videos.title: Who Bought All the RAM in 2026? 🧠
videos.description:
Why are phones and laptops getting more expensive in 2026? The AI memory shortage, explained.
RAM (DRAM) prices are surging as AI data centres buy up memory.

TrendForce says DRAM contract prices rose about 80% in Q2 2026 and about 40% in Q3, with roughly 20% more forecast for Q4 — about three times the start-of-year level if that holds. videos.title: The Coin That Trapped Coca-Cola 🥤
videos.description:
Why did a Coke cost 5 cents for 70 years? The nickel Coke, explained.
How a 1899 bottling deal and nickel-only vending machines froze Coca-Cola's price.

In 1899 two lawyers got Coke's bottling rights with the syrup price fixed permanently. Coke tied its brand to five cents, and its vending machines took a single nickel — the next coin up, a dime, would have doubled the price. Coca-Cola asked the US Treasury for a 7.5-cent coin, and its boss even raised it with his hunting buddy, President Eisenhower. The answer was no. Inflation won, and the nickel Coke was gone by 1959.

videos.description:
Fake FBI "recovery" calls: why scam victims get scammed a second time.
How the IC3 impersonation / fund-recovery scam works, and the one rule that stops it.

After a scam, a second call comes: someone posing as the FBI or its Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) says they can get your money back for a small upfront fee. The FTC warns that recovery scammers buy lists of people who've already been scammed. The FBI (PSA, July 2026) warns of AI deepfake videos of an FBI leader sending victims to a spoofed IC3 site. The real IC3 never contacts you first and never asks for payment to recover lost funds.

videos.title: De Beers' $6.8B Problem 💎
videos.description:
"A Diamond Is Forever": how De Beers made diamonds feel rare, and why lab-grown diamonds are breaking the spell.
Why diamonds resell for so little, explained.

De Beers once controlled most of the world's diamond supply. In 1947 its ad agency, N.W. Ayer, wrote "A Diamond Is Forever" — and "forever" discouraged resale, so few people learned how little a used diamond fetches. Later ads pushed "two months' salary"; the share of US brides with a diamond ring rose from about 10% to about 80% (Al Jazeera). Lab-grown stones now cost up to 80–90% less, and Anglo American has written De Beers down by $6.8 billion since 2023.

videos.title: Someone Bought the Eiffel Tower? 🗼
videos.description:
The man who sold the Eiffel Tower: Victor Lustig's 1925 con, explained.
How a fake government letterhead and a luxury hotel fooled a Paris scrap dealer.

The Eiffel Tower was built on a 20-year permit. In 1925, con man Victor Lustig posed as a government official, invited scrap-metal dealers to the Hôtel de Crillon and said the state would secretly sell the tower for scrap. Dealer André Poisson paid, plus a bribe, and Lustig vanished. Poisson was too embarrassed to go to the police, so Lustig tried the same con again — this time a dealer called the police and he fled. Parts of the story come from later retellings.

videos.title: Stolen in 2017… With a Wheelbarrow? 🪙
videos.description:
The Big Maple Leaf: a 100 kg gold coin stolen from Berlin's Bode Museum with a wheelbarrow, and why its "$1 million" face value was the least valuable thing about it.

In March 2017, thieves climbed in from the railway tracks beside Berlin's Bode Museum and took the Big Maple Leaf, a 100 kg coin of 99.999% gold made by the Royal Canadian Mint. Its face value: one million Canadian dollars. Police put the gold at over $4 million at the time. Investigators believe it was cut up, melted and sold; three men were convicted in 2020 and the coin was never found. At gold's November 2026 price, 100 kg is worth about $13 million.

videos.title: Why Your Eggs Cost More Than Mine 🥚
videos.description:
Dynamic pricing explained: why the same eggs in the same store can show five different prices.
Personalised and algorithmic pricing: Instacart's price tests and AI airline fares.

Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union found that Instacart showed nearly three in four grocery items at more than one price in an experiment; a dozen Lucerne eggs from one Safeway in Washington, D.C. showed $3.99, $4.28, $4.59, $4.69 or $4.79. Instacart ended its item price tests on 22 Dec 2025. Delta has said AI helps set fares on about 3% of its domestic flights, with plans for up to 20%; Delta says it doesn't target individuals with personalised fares. Before a big purchase, compare the price on another app, device or in the store.

videos.title: The Free Trial Trap 💳
videos.description:
Free trial auto-renew: why a "free" trial needs your card, and how companies profit when you forget to cancel.
Subscription traps, hard-to-find cancel buttons, and the Amazon Prime "Iliad" case.

When a free trial ends, the card on file is charged and the plan renews automatically. The US Federal Trade Commission accused Amazon of enrolling people in Prime without clear consent and making cancellation hard; internally the cancel flow was nicknamed "Iliad". Amazon denied wrongdoing but in September 2025 agreed to pay $2.5 billion to settle — a $1 billion civil penalty and $1.5 billion in customer refunds. The fix: set a reminder the day you sign up, and check your statement for charges you don't recognise. Not financial advice.

videos.title: The Job That Pays You… Then Robs You 💸
videos.description:
Task scam explained: the "get paid to like videos" job that ends with you paying them.
How app-optimisation and product-boosting job scams work, and the one rule that beats them.

It starts with an unexpected text or WhatsApp message. You like videos or rate products in sets of 40, an app shows your earnings climbing, and small early payouts make it feel real. Then a "double task" asks you to deposit your own money, usually in crypto, to unlock your earnings. The balance was never real. The FTC counted about 5,000 task-scam reports in all of 2023 and about 20,000 in just the first half of 2024. BBB Scam Tracker puts the median task-scam loss in 2025 at about $2,300. The FTC's rule: never pay to get paid.

videos.title: Why America Killed the Penny 🪙
videos.description:
Why the US stopped making the penny: each one-cent coin cost almost 4 cents to make.
The end of the US penny, and why the nickel loses money too.

In 2024 the US Mint spent about 3.69 cents to make each penny. Pennies had been made since 1793. The Treasury placed its final order for penny blanks in 2025, and the last circulating pennies were struck in Philadelphia on 12 Nov 2025. The nickel costs about 13.78 cents to make and is still being produced. More than 114 billion pennies are still in circulation, and they remain legal tender.

videos.description:
Fake FTC call scam: "Your phone number is linked to a crime and will be deactivated."
How the government-impersonation call moves you from a fake official to a fake police officer to a "security deposit".

On 22 Oct 2026 the US Federal Trade Commission warned about callers posing as FTC officials who say a phone in your name is running scams overseas. They read a fake badge ID, threaten to deactivate your number, transfer you to a fake police officer, ask for your ID and secrecy, then claim you're under arrest unless you pay a "security deposit". The FTC says real employees never ask for money, threats to disconnect your phone are a scam, and requests for secrecy are always a scam. Report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

videos.description:
Are Black Friday deals real? Why most "discounts" are the same price you could pay any other time.
The "was" price trick, countdown clocks, and why prices often drop again after the sale.

Consumer group Which? tracked 175 products at eight big UK retailers from May 2024 to May 2025. 83% were the same price or cheaper at least once outside the Black Friday sale period. videos.title: Infinite Money at the Bottom of the Sea 🌊
videos.description:
Rai stones of Yap: the giant stone money that worked even after one sank to the bottom of the sea.
How stone money on Yap shows what money really is.

On the Pacific island of Yap, money took the form of rai — huge carved stone discs, the largest about 3.6 metres wide and around 4 tonnes. Most were quarried on Palau, roughly 400 km away, and brought back by sea. Big stones were rarely moved; ownership changed by everyone agreeing who owned them. One stone sank on the way home, and the islanders still treated it as existing and kept trading it. Today most of our money is also just numbers that everyone agrees on.

videos.title: How Newton Lost His Fortune! 📉
videos.description:
Isaac Newton and the South Sea Bubble of 1720: how the genius behind gravity lost money in a stock bubble.
Why even smart investors buy at the top.

South Sea Company shares rose from about £130 in January 1720 to over £1,000 by June. Newton sold most of his shares early at a profit, then bought back in at roughly double the price before the crash. Estimates of his loss range from about £10,000 to over £20,000, and historians still debate the evidence. The famous line about calculating the stars but not the madness of people is attributed to him but not confirmed. Not financial advice.

Fake payment screenshot scam: how a "Payment successful" screen can show a green tick when no money was sent.
How shopkeepers get fooled by fake UPI/payment apps, and the one check that stops it.

The Mali emperor's pilgrimage to Mecca and its effect on Cairo's gold price.

On his way to Mecca, Mansa Musa gave gold to Cairo's officials, emirs and treasury, and his party spent freely. videos.title: Was the Rupee Ever Worth $1? 💵
videos.description:
Was 1 rupee equal to 1 dollar in 1947? The rupee vs dollar myth, fact-checked.
Rupee to dollar history: 1947, 1966, 1991 and today's near-record low.

In 1947 the rupee was pegged to the British pound, and a US dollar cost about ₹3.31 — never ₹1. India devalued to ₹7.50 per dollar in 1966, and after the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis the rate passed ₹30 within a year. In May 2026 the rupee hit a record low near ₹97; on 29 Oct 2026 it traded around ₹95. A weaker rupee also makes Indian exports cheaper abroad. Not financial advice.

videos.description:
Digital arrest scam explained: a "police officer" on a video call says you're under arrest — and the only way out is to move your money.
How the fake video-call arrest works, and the one rule that beats it.

One woman in India lost about ₹2.5 crore (~$260,000) in a single week. In 2024, Indians reported over 1.2 lakh digital-arrest cases and lost ₹1,918 crore (over $200 million). Police and agencies do not arrest anyone over a video call, and they never ask you to transfer money. On 29 Oct 2026 India's Supreme Court said banks that miss red flags should compensate victims. videos.title: Why Your $100 Ticket Costs $130 🎟️
videos.description:
Drip pricing shows a low price first and adds mandatory fees at checkout (the $100 to $130 ticket is an illustration). In a large StubHub field experiment (Blake, Moshary, Sweeney & Tadelis; Marketing Science, 2021), users who saw fees only at checkout spent about 21% more and were about 14% more likely to buy. The FTC's Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees, in effect since May 12, 2025, requires live-event ticket sellers and short-term lodging to show the total price, including mandatory fees, up front; taxes and shipping can still be added later. Tip: compare deals on the final checkout total.

videos.title: Tulip Mania 1637: The Bubble That Wasn't? 🌷
videos.description:
Legend says that at the peak of 1637's tulip mania, a single Semper Augustus bulb cost as much as an Amsterdam canal house; its reported price rose from about 1,200 guilders in the 1620s to an asked 10,000 guilders. Bulbs were traded on paper contracts while still in the ground, often in taverns, and in early February 1637 an auction in Haarlem drew no bids and prices collapsed within the week. But historian Anne Goldgar (Tulipmania, 2007) searched the records and could not find anyone who went bankrupt because of tulips; much of the famous drama comes from Charles Mackay's 1841 book. Economist Earl Thompson argued the peak prices reflected contract terms rather than a true bubble.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #tulipmania #history

videos.title: Pay With a Gift Card? It's a Scam. Every Time 🎁
videos.description:
The FTC's rule of thumb: no real business or government agency will ever tell you to pay with a gift card. Scammers pose as the IRS, tech support or a utility about to cut your power, keep you on the phone while you buy cards (sometimes at several stores), then ask for the card number and PIN. With those, the money can be drained within minutes while you're still holding the card, and gift-card payments are hard to trace or reverse. Americans report losing over $200 million a year to gift-card payment scams (FTC Consumer Sentinel data). If someone demands one, hang up and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #scamalert #giftcards

videos.title: Why Zimbabwe Printed a $100 Trillion Note 💵
videos.description:
Zimbabwe issued a 100-trillion-dollar note in January 2009; on its first day it was worth about US$30. In mid-November 2008 monthly inflation was estimated at 79.6 billion percent (Hanke & Kwok, Cato Journal), about 98% a day, with prices doubling roughly every 25 hours. The government removed 25 zeros in three redenominations (2006, 2008, 2009) before suspending the currency in April 2009 in favour of the US dollar and rand. In the 2015 demonetisation, accounts were converted at US$1 per 35 quadrillion Zimbabwe dollars, about 40 cents for a 100-trillion note. Today collectors pay around $100 for an uncirculated one, more than it was ever worth as money.

videos.title: Charles Ponzi Promised 50% in 45 Days 💸
videos.description:
In 1920 Charles Ponzi promised Boston investors 50% in 45 days, supposedly by buying international postal reply coupons cheaply abroad and redeeming them in the US. It couldn't work at scale, so he paid earlier investors with new investors' money. He took in roughly $15 million in about eight months (estimates range from about $10M to $15M; National Archives cites ~$15M). After the Boston Post's investigation, the scheme collapsed in August 1920; investor losses of about $20 million are over $200 million in today's dollars, and the Post won the 1921 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service. Ponzi served prison terms, was deported to Italy in 1934 and died in Rio de Janeiro in 1949.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #PonziScheme #history

videos.title: The $6.50 Popcorn Trick Might Be a Myth 🍿
videos.description:
Why is the medium popcorn priced so close to the large? It may be a decoy: an option that exists to make another one look like a bargain. (The $3 / $6.50 / $7 prices are an illustration.)

The famous evidence is Dan Ariely's account of an Economist offer (web $59, print $125, print + web $125): he reported 84% of his MIT students picked the combo, and only 32% once the print-only option was removed. But that was a classroom exercise, not real subscribers; two of Ariely's other papers have since been retracted over data problems, and larger studies (Journal of Marketing Research, 2014) found the decoy effect weak or absent in many realistic settings. The useful test: would you buy the large without the medium?

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #pricing #psychology

videos.title: Why Prices End in .99 (It's Not the Cents) 🏷️
videos.description:
Why do prices end in .99? The left-digit effect: we read prices left to right and anchor on the first digit, so $9.99 feels like "nine-something" rather than ten.

It shows up in big purchases too: in more than 22 million wholesale used-car auction sales, prices dropped by roughly $150–$200 at each 10,000-mile odometer mark (Lacetera, Pope & Sydnor, NBER). And in a retail field experiment by Anderson (Chicago) and Simester (MIT), a dress sold better at $39 than at $34, suggesting a 9 ending itself signals a bargain. Tip: round up before you decide.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #pricing #psychology

videos.title: Why Costco's Hot Dog Is Still $1.50 🌭
videos.description:
Costco's hot dog and soda combo has cost $1.50 since 1985. Adjusted for inflation it would be around $4.50 today, yet the price hasn't moved, and Costco sold more than 245 million combos in fiscal 2025.

It works as a loss leader: a deal so cheap it brings people in, and getting in takes a membership. In fiscal 2026 Costco earned about $5.9 billion in membership fees against roughly $9.2 billion of net income, so fees are about two-thirds the size of its profit. (The founder's "raise it and I'll kill you" line is the widely told story.)

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #Costco #pricing

videos.title: SEBI Barred 59 for This Stock-Tip Trap 📉
videos.description:
How a stock-tip "pump and dump" works: operators buy a small, cheap stock, a group fills with targets and profit screenshots, and once followers buy, the operators sell to them. The price falls, the group goes quiet, and victims get invited to a new one.

On 22 October 2026 SEBI cautioned investors about unregistered, invite-only WhatsApp groups that use planted members to fake profits. In a 2025 final order in a YouTube-driven pump-and-dump case (Sadhna Broadcast), SEBI barred 59 entities and ordered about ₹58 crore returned. Before trusting any tip, check the adviser's registration on SEBI's website. This is not investment advice. (The ₹500 target and profit screenshots shown are illustrative.)

videos.title: That 70% Off Was Never Real 🏷️
videos.description:
That "70% off" is only as real as the "was" price it's counted from. Before a sale, the crossed-out price can be pushed up, so ₹999 looks like a steal even if it sold for ₹999 all month.

India's amended e-commerce rules (notified September 2026, in force from 1 January 2027) require a discount to be shown next to the "prior price": the lowest price in the 30 days before the sale. EU rules already measure discounts this way, and in an EU check of 314 online traders around Black Friday and Cyber Monday, about 30% still displayed discounts incorrectly. Tip: check a product's price history before you trust the crossed-out number. (The ₹1,999 / ₹999 prices are an illustrative example.)

#Shorts #fakediscount #onlineshopping

videos.title: Milka Shrank 10%. Did You Notice? 🍫
videos.description:
Milka bars in Germany went from 100 g to 90 g in the same wrapper. That's shrinkflation: the price rise you don't see on the tag.

Why it works: in US store data (NielsenIQ, 2010–2020), a 1% price rise cut sales about 1.2%, but a 1% size cut hurt sales only about half as much. After a downsize, the price per unit rose about 12% on average. In 2016 Toblerone widened the gaps between its peaks, and in May 2026 a German court (Bremen) ruled the Milka cut misleading. The fix: compare the price per kilo, not the price tag.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_ZvJ7AW55-k

The phrase has a famous story. In 1807, a writer named William Cobbett used it. He told of a boy using a red herring to throw hounds off a hare's trail. Here's the twist. Language experts say the story was probably made up. Real hunters used a smelly drag to train dogs, not to mislead them. Historians find no sign of hunters using one that way. Why it works: a new topic is interesting, and it relieves the pressure to answer. Everyone is grateful to stop feeling cornered. So nobody notices the dodge. The defence: say, interesting, and the biscuit? Bring the conversation back to the question. Fallacy ten. No true Scotsman. Sam says, no kind person would ever want the last biscuit. Pat says, but I am kind, and I would like it. Sam says, then you are not really kind.

videos.title: The planes that never returned #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ssr-s652pHw

In 1943, a mathematician named Abraham Wald was working in a group at Columbia University. As the story is told, he looked at the places with no holes. Where the holes were, the plane could take it. Planes hit there never came back, so those hits never got counted. The silent, missing planes were telling the real story. Wald's real memos are on record. The popular retellings add some details. So treat the neat story with a pinch of salt, and keep the lesson. This is called survivorship bias. You only see the ones that made it back. That's why every success story hides ten thousand quiet failures. Nobody writes the book called, I Tried Everything And It Flopped. So ask who isn't in the data, and why.

videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uS6ZeKSzIXo

In 1968, Robert Knox and James Inkster interviewed bettors at racetracks in British Columbia. Some were asked just before placing a $2 bet. Others, just after. The horse hadn't changed. The odds hadn't changed. Yet the ones who'd already bet felt more confident their horse would win. You've felt this after hitting buy. Suddenly the good reviews look more convincing. Once the choice can't be undone, the only thing left to change is your mind. Stage three is the story. This is where those four doors swing open. You collect reasons it was right. You shrink the parts that hurt.

videos.title: What 80 percent missed #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ai8fO7ty4ho

In a 2016 Stanford study, researchers showed middle schoolers a sponsored article. More than 80 percent took it for real news. Some even noticed the sponsored label, and still believed it was news. That suggests a label alone isn't doing the job. Why does it work? We trust the format. If it looks like news, we treat it as news. The giveaway is small: a faint label, a different colour, a tiny corner mark. Before you click, ask what that button is actually promising. Friend spam. A new app asks to find your friends. It sounds helpful, so you tap allow. Find your friends sounds like a favour to you. Then your whole contact list gets invitations, written as if from you.

videos.title: The no button gone #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ai8fO7ty4ho

In 2020, Midas Nouwens and colleagues studied the five biggest consent tools. They scraped 680 popular UK sites. Only 11.8 percent met even the minimum requirements of European law. In a small experiment with 40 people, they removed the reject button from page one. Consent rose by 22 to 23 percentage points. Why does it work? The easy path usually wins. So a hard no hardly gets chosen. Nobody forces you. They only make one road smooth and the other muddy. Compare the two buttons. If one is easy and one is hidden, someone designed that. One question catches nearly all of these. Would this still work if both choices looked equal and were written plainly?

videos.title: The prime cancel maze #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ai8fO7ty4ho

In June 2023, the US Federal Trade Commission sued Amazon over Prime. The agency said joining took one or two clicks. It said cancelling took four pages, six clicks and fifteen options. Amazon's own name for that process was Iliad. Those were allegations, and Amazon disputed them. Remember, this was a settlement, not a verdict on every claim. In September 2025, three days into the trial, Amazon settled for $2.5 billion. That's a $1 billion penalty. Plus $1.5 billion in refunds, to about 35 million people. Here's why it works: every extra step is a small chance to give up.

videos.title: Paid less, believed more #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uS6ZeKSzIXo

In 1959, Festinger and James Carlsmith ran an experiment at Stanford University. Seventy-one male students took part. Each spent about an hour on dull tasks, like turning pegs on a board. It was boring on purpose. That was the whole point. Then each student was asked a favour. Tell the next student it was interesting. Some were paid $1 to tell that lie. Others were paid $20. Afterwards, they were asked how much they had really enjoyed the tasks. So who believed their own lie? Most people guess the twenty-dollar group. On a scale from minus five to plus five, the answer went the other way.

videos.title: The prison, rerun #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-56v2Z4AXRw

Then, in 2002, someone tried to run the prison again. Psychologists Alex Haslam and Stephen Reicher ran the BBC Prison Study, shown on British television. Fifteen men were randomly made guards or prisoners. This time, the researchers didn't tell the guards how to behave. The guards never fully embraced their power. Some wanted to befriend the prisoners instead. They argued, lacked leadership, and worked against each other. The prisoners did the opposite. They banded together and challenged the guards. And over time, their depression and burnout went down. Zimbardo rejected it as a real replication.

videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q_OEuDAT3x8

In 2004, Constantine Sedikides and colleagues asked whether normal narcissists are psychologically healthy. Across five studies, it went with less sadness, less loneliness and less anxiety. It even went with better well-being for couples. In daily diaries, people higher in normal narcissism reported less sadness. But here's the catch. Self-esteem explained the whole link. Why does it work? The benefit only came with genuine self-esteem. Healthy pride can laugh at itself, and still feel fine. It's confidence that doesn't need anyone else to shrink. The fragile kind has to win every room just to feel okay. The healthy kind can lose an argument and still feel fine. So how do you tell which one you're facing?

videos.title: The faked breakdown #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-56v2Z4AXRw

The most famous moment is a prisoner screaming in his cell, caught on tape. It happened about thirty-six hours in, and he was soon released. His name was Douglas Korpi, prisoner eighty-six twelve. Decades later, he gave writer Ben Blum a very different account. He'd taken the job hoping to sit around by himself and study for his graduate exams. But the guards wouldn't let him have his textbooks. He says he tried faking a stomach ache first. That didn't work. So, by his own account, he faked the breakdown. He told Blum, anybody who is a clinician would know that I was faking.

videos.title: Eleven rules, copied #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-56v2Z4AXRw

What he found starts in May 1971, in a Stanford dorm called Toyon Hall. Five students in one of Zimbardo's classes had picked prisons as their project topic. They ran a weekend mock prison, with six guards, six prisoners and a student warden. Zimbardo was very interested when they presented it, and asked them for a report. That student leader went on to serve as the warden of the famous study. Here's the striking part. The Stanford Prison Experiment had seventeen rules. Eleven of them were copied directly from the dorm experiment. The other six were adapted to the new space and the longer stay.

videos.title: The kindest narcissist #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q_OEuDAT3x8

In 2012, a team led by Jochen Gebauer published a study on it. They split narcissism in two: the kind about power, and the kind about goodness. A classic thought for the second kind is: I am the most helpful person. They built a questionnaire to measure it, the Communal Narcissism Inventory. Communal narcissists rated themselves high on warmth and kindness. They saw themselves as the most caring people they knew. But the people around them didn't rate them that way. Why does it work on you? We don't question someone who seems generous. The kindness can be real. The point of it is the applause. Notice whether their good deeds ever happen when nobody's looking. Antagonistic narcissism. The rival in every room. You get a promotion, and they congratulate you through gritted teeth.

videos.title: The crowd was wrong #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s44tK7-B3nI

In 1951, psychologist Solomon Asch ran a famous experiment at Swarthmore College. Everyone but one person was secretly in on it, and gave the wrong answer. Then it was the real volunteer's turn to answer out loud. About three in four volunteers went along with the crowd at least once. Across all the wrong-answer trials, about a third of answers followed the group. The line was obvious. The crowd was louder than their own eyes. Some volunteers doubted themselves. Others simply didn't want to stand out. And a few never bent, not once. That matters too. But here's the thing: the crowd wasn't pushing. It was simply there. It works because disagreeing feels like risk, and agreeing feels like safety. Ask who is counting the crowd, and who benefits from the count.

videos.title: The same wine twice #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WB8PU4FKPns

In 2008, Hilke Plassmann and colleagues scanned people while they tasted wine. The same wine was presented once as $5 and once as $45. People rated the $45 version as tastier. A pleasure region, the medial orbitofrontal cortex, was more active too. It wasn't pretending. The price seemed to change the experience itself. A high tag can make something feel special before you try it. Ask yourself whether you could tell the difference blind. Pricey isn't wrong. It just isn't proof. The soundtrack. You pass the wine shelf, and an accordion is playing. You reach for a French bottle, and don't ask yourself why. You may even hum along. It's only a speaker, but it changes who leaves with what. This is called the in-store music effect, tested in a British supermarket.

videos.title: One cent changed it all #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WB8PU4FKPns

In 2007, Shampanier, Mazar and Ariely offered a Hershey's Kiss or a Lindt truffle. At the first set of prices, only 27 percent chose the Kiss. They cut both prices by one cent, so the Kiss became free. One cent. That's all it took to change the whole choice. The gap between the two stayed exactly the same. Yet the share choosing the Kiss jumped from 27 to 69 percent. Free doesn't feel like a lower price. It feels risk-free. The researchers suggest that zero removes the sting of a possible loss. Free gifts and free trials lean on exactly that feeling. Free can come with a form, an email address or a renewing trial. Ask what the free thing is steering you toward buying next. Free is still a price.

videos.title: Liked, then disliked #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q_OEuDAT3x8

In 1998, psychologist Delroy Paulhus tracked how people in discussion groups rated each other. Groups of four to six met seven times, twenty minutes each. After meeting one, the self-enhancers were rated agreeable, competent and well adjusted. By meeting seven, the same people were rated negatively. And they still saw themselves as wonderful. Nobody else did. The charm burns bright, then it burns out. First impressions are fast, and confidence looks like competence. Judge someone on meeting seven, not meeting one. Vulnerable narcissism. The quiet one, often called covert. You reply to their message with one word, because you're busy. By evening they've gone cold, and you're apologising without knowing why. Soon you're managing their moods, walking on eggshells.

videos.title: The frank statement #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s44tK7-B3nI

On the fourth of January, 1954, a full-page notice ran in newspapers across America. It appeared in 448 papers in 258 cities, an estimated 43 million readers. It was called A Frank Statement to Cigarette Smokers. Fourteen tobacco companies and trade groups signed it. The notice promised to support honest research. The research body was paid for by the industry itself. It questioned the research linking smoking to lung cancer. And it announced a new body, the Tobacco Industry Research Committee. This is called card stacking. Everything said may be true. What's missing is the point. A flashlight lights up what you want seen, and nothing else. The rest of the room stays dark. The honest question is always what's in the dark.

videos.title: The dress that sold more #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WB8PU4FKPns

In 2003, Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester ran field experiments on women's clothing. Customers got the same dress at different prices. Nothing else changed. The catalogues went to real customers, with real money on the line. A dress at $39 outsold the same dress at $34. By roughly a third, according to summaries of the paper. Customers paid five dollars more, and more of them bought. So how can paying more feel like paying less? One idea is that we read nine as a bargain. Researchers call it the left-digit effect. The front digit does the work. The dress never changed. Only the way your eye read the tag. It's a trick of attention, and attention is yours to redirect. One line at the end of this video beats every trick here.

videos.description:

Later researchers found Milgram ran even more versions than the book describes. One unpublished version used friends and relatives as pairs. So obedience isn't a fixed trait. videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w834GRbEl3U

In 2016, Roy Lewicki, Beth Polin and Robert Lount tested six parts of an apology. Across two experiments, 755 people judged apologies with anywhere from one to all six parts. More parts worked better than fewer. Taking responsibility ranked as the most important. Owning it, without a single qualifier. An offer to repair the harm came second. Not just feelings. A plan to fix it. That matches Lazare. Say what you did. Show you understand how it landed. Repair it. Picture the friend who missed your birthday, trying again properly. "I missed it. videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w834GRbEl3U

First they deny it. Then they attack you. Then they play the wounded one. Somehow, the chairs have swapped places. Say you politely mention your sister missed the third promise. She says, "wow, you're always attacking me. Do you know how hard I try?" Ten minutes later, you're offering reassurance. The clipboard is forgotten. Psychologist Jennifer Freyd named that sequence DARVO: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender. In 2017, Sarah Harsey, Eileen Zurbriggen and Freyd studied what happens when people are confronted. They found DARVO was commonly reported, and its three parts tended to appear together.

videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ST2rqtmY9zs

Four times, a man in a grey coat used the same push. Three of his pushes worked. The fourth, people refused. That fourth push was the only one that sounded like an actual order. Think about that, because it breaks the story you were told. So why would a flat order fail when everyone says orders rule? The textbook version is simple. Ordinary people will do terrible things when an authority tells them to. But the records say something different, and it's far more useful. The story is stranger, and it matters for your phone, your job, and your bank. I'll show you what the original study found, and what it didn't.

videos.title: The one line reply #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vVIOPweaiIk

When someone brings you a long complaint about another person, pause. You can say: that sounds important. Have you told them? That one line returns the problem to its owner. If the message is about you, answer calmly and directly. Try: I'd like to hear that from them. Can we talk, just the two of us? You can also say: I'm not going to discuss them when they're not here. Offer a direct conversation, and see whether it is accepted. If it is, the pattern may have been fear, not strategy. If it's refused again and again, that tells you something too. Keep notes of what was said, by whom, and when. Because triangulation often sits next to other control, and it can wear you down. If you feel frightened, controlled or cut off from people, tell someone you trust. A domestic abuse helpline in your country can talk it through, no judgement.

In 2009, Cheryl Buehler and Deborah Welsh studied 416 families. They followed young people aged 11 to 15 across four annual waves. In the second, 83 people read conflicts where the apology came early, late, or never. Apologies landed best after the hurt person felt heard and understood. Being heard first seems to matter. Quick isn't always bad.

videos.title: When guilt backfires #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qSByyrUM9cQ

In 1995, researchers Coulter and Pinto tested guilt in advertising. They showed ads to 60 working mothers, a group often targeted with guilt. Moderate guilt appeals produced more guilt than weak ones, or strong ones. A middle amount works. Too little barely registers. Strong appeals produced anger, and worse attitudes toward the brand. Pile it on too high, and people stop feeling guilty. They feel pushed. The harder the shove, the more people push back. Pressure breeds resistance. That's why the guilt-tripper who escalates often loses the very closeness they wanted. Psychologists call that reactance: you resist because you were pressured. So heavy guilt backfires.

videos.title: Why three beats two #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vVIOPweaiIk

In the 1950s and 60s, a psychiatrist named Murray Bowen studied whole families. He watched how people behaved together, not just one patient alone. In 1966, he published a paper describing something he called the emotional triangle. His idea was simple. A relationship between two people is fragile. When tension rises, two people can only carry so much of it. So they pull in a third, and the tension spreads across three lines. Bowen called the triangle the smallest stable relationship system. Two legs wobble. Three stand. In calm times, two are the close insiders and one is the outsider. And the outsider tends to work hard to get back in. Think of tension like heat in a small room. A third person is an open window. Even a pet or a hobby can become the third corner.

videos.title: A lie and a favour #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qSByyrUM9cQ

In 1967, Jonathan Freedman and colleagues made people tell a small lie. Later, a stranger asked them for an unpaid favour. 20 of the 31 guilty people said yes, against 11 in the comparison group. Nobody pressured them. The feeling alone did the pushing. Feelings can push hard. They said yes to a person they would never meet again. In 1972, Dennis Regan's team went further. They made people think they'd broken a camera, by accident. Then a stranger walked past with an open bag. The guilty group was more likely to spot the problem and help than the others. They hadn't done anything wrong. They felt guilty, so they helped. Guilt pushes you toward repair, even when nothing needs repairing.

videos.title: The smoke alarm idea #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qSByyrUM9cQ

Think of guilt as a smoke alarm for your relationships. Now imagine someone setting it off when there's no fire. Everyone in the house reacts, even though nothing is burning. That's a guilt trip. It borrows the alarm to move you. The same Baumeister team's 1995 paper looked at people's own stories about guilt. They found that inducing guilt looks like a costly but effective way to influence a partner. So it keeps getting used, because it keeps paying off. Costly, because it can sour the relationship. Effective, because it often works. It's a bit like a cracked cup: it still works, but it leaks. Every use cuts a little at the trust between two people. In 1991, researchers Anita Vangelisti, John Daly and Janine Rudnick asked how people do it.

videos.title: The leaving test #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VgWEy7Rye0E

Practise a gentle no, because the first small yes is where it starts. It feels rude at first, and that rudeness is just the habit changing. You can say, I'd like to think it over, and take a week. Real friendships survive a week of waiting. Pressure doesn't. If someone insists you decide tonight, that urgency is worth noticing. If someone you love is in a group like this, stay warm and keep in touch.

Early humans had no alarm clocks, so how did they wake up? ⏰ Dawn light reaching the body through closed eyelids tells the body clock it’s morning, melatonin falls and the hormone cortisol rises. Body temperature also bottoms out in the early hours, then climbs before waking. Historians have found records of a “first sleep” and “second sleep” in pre-industrial Europe, though studies of modern hunter-gatherers mostly show one main sleep period. A study of the Hadza in Tanzania also found people rarely slept in sync, which led to the sentinel hypothesis: someone may always have kept watch.

videos.title: 5 Great Strategists — The Decisions That Changed History
videos.description:
Before a great battle is won on the field, it is usually won by a decision that looks like a mistake. videos.title: The 80/20 Rule for Your Career | Do Less, Achieve More
videos.description:
Most of what you do every day barely matters — and a tiny fraction of it matters more than everything else combined. You could work ten hours a day, answer every email, attend every meeting, check every box — and still go nowhere. Or you could find the few things that actually move your career forward, and do those relentlessly.

This is the 80/20 rule: about 80 percent of your results come from about 20 percent of your effort. It started with an Italian economist, Vilfredo Pareto, in 1896 — 80 percent of Italy's land owned by 20 percent of the people — and it applies to your career more than anywhere else: your tasks, your skills, and your people.

In this video: which tasks are leverage and which are just maintenance, the few skills that actually drive your income, the handful of relationships that produce most of your opportunities, a one-week audit to find your own 20 percent, and a 7-day plan to start using it today.

Goal-Based Investing: The Wealth Strategy That Actually Matches Your Life
videos.description:
For decades, the financial industry judged investment success by a single, narrow metric: did your portfolio beat the S&P 500? Wall Street advisors pushed clients into rigid, one-size-fits-all asset allocations designed to maximize risk-adjusted returns against a market benchmark. videos.title: Black-Litterman & Beyond: How Goldman Sachs Fixed Modern Portfolio Theory
videos.description: For nearly four decades after Harry Markowitz introduced Modern Portfolio Theory, institutional asset managers ran into the same frustrating real-world failure: Markowitz mean-variance optimizers are "error maximizers." If your historical return estimate for a stock is off by just half a percent, the optimizer will assign absurd, extreme weights—allocating eighty percent of your portfolio to a single volatile asset and completely destroying diversification.In the early 1990s, legendary quantitative researchers Fischer Black and Robert Litterman at Goldman Sachs solved this problem by creating the Black-Litterman Model. Instead of relying on noisy historical averages, Black-Litterman uses Bayesian probability to reverse-engineer the market's implied equilibrium returns, allowing investors to gently blend in their own subjective market views with explicit confidence levels. In the foreign exchange market, where over seven trillion dollars trade every single day, currency exchange rates do not move based on simple retail sentiment or casual speculation. The fundamental pricing of forward exchange contracts is governed by one of the most bedrock mathematical laws in international finance: Interest Rate Parity (IRP).

Interest Rate Parity states a simple, elegant principle: the difference in interest rates between two countries should equal the spread between the current spot exchange rate and the forward exchange rate. If this relationship broke down, institutional banks and algorithmic hedge funds could borrow cheaply in one currency, convert it to a higher-yielding currency, hedge the exchange rate risk in the forward market, and generate infinite risk-free arbitrage profits. In real financial markets, nominal yields are an illusion; the only metric that dictates true wealth generation and controls global asset prices is the Real Yield.

videos.title: Sovereign & Credit Spreads: How Bond Markets Price Financial Panic
videos.description:
In financial markets, the stock market is often noisy, emotional, and prone to wild narrative swings. But when professional risk managers, macro hedge funds, and central bankers want an unfiltered, real-time measure of systemic risk and corporate solvency, they look directly at the bond market: specifically, at Sovereign and Credit Spreads.

A credit spread is simply the extra yield an investor demands to hold risky debt—such as corporate bonds or peripheral government paper—over a risk-free benchmark like US Treasuries or German Bunds. When spreads are compressed and razor-thin, capital is abundant and risk is ignored. But when economic stress, default fears, or liquidity freezes hit the financial system, credit spreads widen violently long before equity markets acknowledge the danger. In this macroeconomic masterclass, we break down how to read credit and sovereign spreads like an institutional risk manager. We examine the classic Bund-to-OAT and Bund-to-BTP spreads across Europe, decode high-yield OAS (Option-Adjusted Spread) as a recession alarm, and explore how credit spreads serve as the ultimate early warning system for market crashes.

💡 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

What Is a Credit Spread: The mathematical yield premium demanded for bearing default, duration, and liquidity risk over benchmark sovereign debt.

Option-Adjusted Spread (OAS): How institutional investors strip out embedded call options to measure the pure credit risk of corporate bonds.

videos.title: Why good-looking people seem smarter (Halo Effect) #Shorts

videos.title: Can a Bigger Spoon Make You Take Two-Thirds More Candy? | Blind Spot #38
videos.description:
What decides how much candy you grab? Not your stomach. The spoon.

In 2006, psychologists at the University of Pennsylvania put a big bowl of candy in the lobby of an apartment building. A sign said "Eat your fill" and asked people to use the spoon to serve themselves. On some days the spoon was a tablespoon; on others it was a scoop four times as big. People who didn't know they were being observed took more candy with the big scoop: about two-thirds more, according to press coverage of the study. Same bowl, same sign, same lobby. Only the spoon changed.

That's unit bias: we treat one unit of food (one scoop, one plate, one bag) as the appropriate amount, whatever size it is. Note that the study measured candy taken, not eaten.

Our examples (the giant movie popcorn, the "single" slice, the "family size" chips) are comic illustrations, not findings from the study.

How to catch it: shrink the unit before you start. A smaller bowl, a smaller plate, pour some out and put the bag away. Your brain will still count it as "one".

Previous: #37 Reciprocity
Next: #39 (follow so you don't miss it)

videos.title: Does "Saves 200" Beat "400 Are Lost"? Same Plan | Blind Spot #12
videos.description:
In 1981, Tversky and Kahneman gave people a puzzle: a new disease threatens 600 people, pick a plan. One group heard "the sure plan saves 200" and most took it. Another group heard "400 are lost" and most ran to the gamble. Do the math: it's the exact same plan, only the words changed.

That's the framing effect: your brain reacts to the wrapping before it checks what's inside. "75% lean" beef tasted better than "25% fat" beef. Same beef. A "pre-owned" car. An ex who isn't jobless, just "exploring options".

Ten families share one green meadow. Nobody owns the grass. Then one herder does some quiet math, and a perfectly sensible choice starts to spread. This is an imagined village from an 1833 lecture, told as a short picture-book story.

videos.title: A Free Shortcut Is Added. Does Traffic Get Faster? | Blind Spot M17
videos.description:
Four thousand drivers. Two roads. Each road has a narrow bridge that jams and a highway that always takes 45 minutes. Split evenly, every trip takes 65 minutes. Now the city builds a free shortcut between the two roads. Do trips get faster, stay the same, or get slower? Watch what a car-by-car count says.

Why does the obvious answer fail? Every driver checks only their own trip, never what the whole crowd does at the same time. Mathematician Dietrich Braess described this effect in 1968, and it still shapes how engineers think about road networks. The simple habit that catches it: before taking a shortcut, ask what happens if everybody does.

Last answer (from M16, the coin rotation paradox): a coin half as wide spins 3 times around a big coin, two from rolling along the edge plus one for the trip around.

In 1980, psychologist Neil Weinstein asked college students to compare their own chances of good and bad life events with those of their classmates. Good things: "more likely for me." Bad things: "less likely for me."

videos.title: The Coin Puzzle That Fooled a Famous Exam | Blind Spot M16
videos.description:
Two identical coins. One sits still. The other rolls around it, no slipping, all the way back to the start. How many times does the rolling coin spin? Your gut gives one answer. Watch the arrow and count.

Why does the count surprise almost everyone? A rolling coin turns for two different reasons, and your brain only notices one of them. In 1982 a big American exam, the SAT, asked a version of this question, and the answer key was wrong. Earth hides the same trick in plain sight: it spins about 366 times a year, but you only get 365 sunsets.

Last answer (from M15, the sunflower's golden angle): turn exactly 144 degrees between seeds and you get five straight spokes, because 144 degrees is two fifths of a turn.

videos.title: The Weirdest Angle in Nature: Why Sunflowers Turn 137.5° | Blind Spot M15
videos.description:
Drop a seed. Turn. Drop the next one a bit farther out. Which turn packs the seeds tightest? A quarter turn gives four straight lines. A half turn gives two. 140 degrees gives 18 spokes. 137.5 degrees gives no spokes and no holes: every seed gets its own space. Add just one degree and the spokes and gaps come back.

That's the golden angle: 360° x (2 - golden ratio) = 137.5077...°. In 1979 H. Vogel showed that this one rule (seed k at angle k x 137.5° and distance proportional to the square root of k) draws a sunflower head. The golden ratio is the hardest number to approximate with fractions, so no number of turns brings a seed back onto an old seed's line. In 1992 Douady and Couder dripped tiny magnetic drops into oil; the drops pushed each other apart and spiraled at nearly the same angle. Nobody told them.

Last answer (from M14, Penney's game): your friend picks tails-tails-tails, you pick heads-tails-tails, and you win 7 times out of 8.

videos.title: Pick First? You Lose. The Coin Game Rigged by Math | Blind Spot M14
videos.description:
Flip a fair coin until you see heads, heads, tails (HHT) or heads, tails, tails (HTT). First to show up wins. Both patterns take exactly 8 flips on average. Same wait. So it's 50/50, right? Nope: HHT wins two races out of three. Watch 10,000 races.

In 1969 Walter Penney turned this into a bet: you pick any three flips, your friend picks second, and your friend can always pick a pattern that beats yours. Pick heads-heads-heads? Tails-heads-heads wins 7 times out of 8. The cheat code: copy their first two flips and put the opposite of their middle flip in front. There is no best pick: THH beats HHT, HHT beats HTT, HTT beats TTH, TTH beats THH. It's rock, paper, scissors with pocket change. If someone kindly lets you pick first, ask why.

Last answer (from M13, the chaos game with a square): the dots just fill the square evenly, like TV static. No picture.

videos.title: He Made the Right Call. Everyone Called Him an Idiot. | Blind Spot
videos.description:
One yard from winning the Super Bowl, a coach called a pass. It was intercepted, and the headlines called it the worst call in Super Bowl history. Had the same pass been caught, the same call would have been called genius. Nothing changed except where the ball landed. From that spot (second down at the 1-yard line) passes were intercepted only about 2 times in 100.

That's outcome bias: we judge a decision by how it ended, not by what the person knew when they made it. Poker player and author Annie Duke calls it "resulting". In 1988, Jonathan Baron and John Hershey gave students written descriptions of risky decisions, such as a heart operation. The decision information was the same; when the outcome was bad, people rated the decision worse and the decision maker less competent.

It works the other way too: a bad choice that happened to work out (driving home after a few drinks) can feel like skill. Please don't treat that as a good call.

How to catch it: cover up the ending. Ask what they knew then. Was it a good bet?

A fair note: the headline wording and the "caught pass" headline are illustrations, not exact quotes, and the interception rate varies by source and by how narrowly the situation is defined. The driver, lottery and plan examples are illustrations, not research findings.

videos.title: She Never Said a Word, Yet Got More Attractive | Blind Spot #32
videos.description:
Can you become more attractive by doing absolutely nothing? In one classic classroom study, kind of, yes.

In 1992, psychologists Richard Moreland and Scott Beach sent four women of similar appearance into a big college lecture. The one rule: sit there, say nothing, talk to no one. One woman never came to class. The others attended 5, 10 or 15 sessions. At the end of the term, students rated pictures of all four. The more sessions a woman had sat through, the more attractive, likeable and similar to themselves the students rated her, even though, according to summaries of the study, they had little memory of seeing her.

That's the mere exposure effect: just seeing something again makes you like it more. Robert Zajonc named it in 1968 after finding that made-up words, symbols and faces were liked more the more often people had seen them. One explanation is that familiar things are easy for the brain to process, and we mistake "easy" for "good".

Our examples are jokes, not data: the song you hated until the radio played it all summer, the coworker who grew on you, the ex who just felt familiar.

How to catch it: when something feels right, ask, "Is it good, or just familiar?" Then give the new option a few more looks.

Previous: #31 Overjustification Effect
Next: #33 (follow so you don't miss it)

Sources:
• R. L. Moreland & S. R. Beach, "Exposure effects in the classroom: The development of affinity among students", Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 28(3), 255-276, 1

videos.title: Why a Prize Made Kids Stop Loving Drawing | Blind Spot #31
videos.description:
Want a kid to stop loving drawing? Easy. Give them a prize for it.

In 1973, researchers at Stanford found preschoolers who already loved drawing with felt-tip markers during free play. Then they made three groups. Group one was promised a "Good Player" certificate with a ribbon. Group two got the same certificate as a surprise. Group three got nothing.

One to two weeks later, the markers came back with no prizes. The surprise kids and the no-prize kids kept drawing. The kids who had been promised the ribbon drew about half as much as the others.

That's the overjustification effect: once a reward shows up, your brain decides you did it for the reward, not for fun. It's the hobby you turned into a side hustle, the step app that made walks feel like homework, the chores you only do for cash.

How to catch it: before you add a prize, ask "Did I already love this?" If yes, just say thanks.

Note: the effect is real but debated in size and reach. It shows up mainly for rewards that are promised in advance and tied to doing the task; a surprise reward and simple praise did not hurt. The examples in the video are illustrations, not study results.

videos.title: Why Your $1 Lottery Ticket Feels Worth $9 | Blind Spot #30
videos.description:
How does a one-dollar lottery ticket become worth almost nine dollars? You pick it yourself.

In 1975, psychologist Ellen Langer ran a small office lottery. Tickets cost $1 each, and each one was a football player card. Half the workers got to choose their card; the others were simply handed one. Same price, same odds, pure luck. Before the drawing, each person was asked what they would sell their ticket for. People who were handed a card asked for about $2 on average ($1.96). People who picked their own card asked for almost $9 ($8.67). For a random card.

That's the illusion of control: when you get to choose, your brain feels like your hand is on the wheel, even when the wheel spins by itself. It's the same pull behind pressing the elevator button five times, blowing on the dice, or wearing lucky socks on game day.

Fair warning: Langer's study was small (53 people) and from 1975, and a large 2021 project (17 experiments, 10,825 people, using a variety of measures rather than an exact copy of Langer's test) found that choice rarely creates a feeling of control on its own. We keep the 1975 numbers as history, and the everyday habit is still very real.

How to catch it: ask "Would the odds change if someone else picked?" If not, let it go.

videos.title: Random Dots Draw a Perfect Triangle? The Chaos Game | Blind Spot M13
videos.description:
Draw a triangle. Put a dot anywhere inside. Roll a die: 1 or 2, jump halfway to the top corner; 3 or 4, halfway to the left; 5 or 6, halfway to the right. Drop a dot. Roll again. Pure luck. So what picture do 10,000 dots make: a blob, static, or a pattern? Watch. Triangles inside triangles inside triangles, from pure luck.

That is the chaos game, named by mathematician Michael Barnsley in his 1988 book Fractals Everywhere. The picture is the Sierpinski triangle, described by Waclaw Sierpinski in 1915. And here is the creepy part: after the very first jump, not one dot ever lands in the big middle hole. Our brain thinks random means messy. But the die is random and the rule is not. Barnsley even grew a fern this way: four rules, random picks.

Why the hole stays empty (our own short proof): if P is anywhere inside the big triangle and A is a corner, the halfway point (P + A) / 2 lies in the half-size copy of the triangle at corner A. The three corner copies never touch the open middle hole, so every dot after the first jump avoids it, forever.

How the video was made: everything is our own animation. The die is a seeded random generator; each new dot is (old dot + chosen corner) / 2. The counters are real: the dot counter shows how many dots were drawn (up to 100,000) and the "in the hole" counter counts the dots that really landed in the hole, and honestly reads 0. The dots take the colour of the corner they just jumped to. The fern uses Barnsley's four maps with chances 1%,

videos.title: The "Worst Call Ever" Was the Right Call? | Blind Spot #41
videos.description:
One yard from winning the Super Bowl, a coach called a pass. It was intercepted, and the headlines called it the worst call in Super Bowl history. Had the same pass been caught, the same call would have been called genius. Nothing changed except where the ball landed. From that spot (second down at the 1-yard line) passes were intercepted only about 2 times in 100.

That's outcome bias: we judge a decision by how it ended, not by what the person knew when they made it. Poker player and author Annie Duke calls it "resulting". In 1988, Jonathan Baron and John Hershey gave students written descriptions of risky decisions, such as a heart operation. The decision information was the same; when the outcome was bad, people rated the decision worse and the decision maker less competent.

It works the other way too: a bad choice that happened to work out (driving home after a few drinks) can feel like skill. Please don't treat that as a good call.

How to catch it: cover up the ending. Ask what they knew then. Was it a good bet?

A fair note: the headline wording and the "caught pass" headline are illustrations, not exact quotes, and the interception rate varies by source and by how narrowly the situation is defined. The driver, lottery and plan examples are illustrations, not research findings.

videos.title: Same 6 Words, Opposite Order, Different Person | Blind Spot #40
videos.description:
In 1946, psychologist Solomon Asch read two groups of people a list of six traits about a stranger: intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn, envious. The second group heard the exact same words in reverse order. The group that heard "intelligent" first formed a clearly more favorable impression; the group that heard "envious" first saw a person whose problems outweighed his talents. Nothing added, nothing taken out, just the order.

That's the primacy effect: your brain makes up its mind early, then reads everything after through that first impression. "Stubborn" after "smart" sounds like principles; "stubborn" after "envious" just sounds like trouble.

A fair caveat: a modern replication of Asch's order manipulation found a smaller effect than the classic result, and a 2020 study using videos of real behavior found no primacy effect at all. Word lists are one thing; real life is messier. The interview, dating-profile and first-day examples in the video are illustrations, not proven findings.

How to catch it: when you judge someone, flip the list in your head. Would you still think this if you'd heard the bad stuff first? And when you're the list, lead with your best.

videos.title: 93% Said They're Top-Half Drivers. Math Says No | Blind Spot #39
videos.description:
How can 93% of people be in the top half? They can't. That's the whole problem.

In 1981, Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson asked student drivers in the USA and in Sweden to rate their own driving skill compared with the other people in the study, from the least to the most skillful. In the US group, 93% rated themselves above the median driver. In the Swedish group it was 69%. The top half can only hold 50%, so even the modest answer was too many.

That's the better-than-average effect (also called illusory superiority): we judge ourselves from the inside, by our intentions, and everyone else from the outside, by their worst moments. A 2023 preregistered replication with 1,203 participants found the same pattern again.

Our examples (the group project, the dating profile, the "cool boss") are illustrations, not findings from the study. The Sweden joke is just a joke.

How to catch it: pick something you think you're great at. Ask "Better than who, exactly?" Then ask someone who has actually watched you do it (not your mom).

videos.title: A Free Soda Doubled This Stranger's Sales | Blind Spot #37
videos.description:
In 1971, psychologist Dennis Regan invited students to what they thought was an art study: rate some paintings alongside another "student", Joe. Joe was really an actor. On a short break he either came back with two Cokes, one for the participant, or came back with nothing. Later he asked a favor: would they buy some raffle tickets? People who had received the unrequested soda bought about twice as many tickets, even when they didn't particularly like Joe.

That's reciprocity: your brain keeps score, and an unpaid favor feels like a debt. The free sample, the "free gift" with every sign-up, the friend who helped you move and now "owns" your Saturdays.

How to catch it: when someone hands you something you didn't ask for, say thanks. Then decide as if the gift never happened. "Thank you" doesn't have to mean "yes."

videos.title: They Were Told What to Write. Readers Blamed Them Anyway | Blind Spot #34
videos.description:
If someone is forced to argue a side, do you believe they mean it? You shouldn't. You will.

In 1967, psychologists Edward Jones and Victor Harris had Duke University students read short essays about Fidel Castro. Some essays praised him, some attacked him. Readers then guessed what each writer really thought. Some were told the writer chose the side freely. Others were told the side was assigned, so the writer had no choice. When the side was chosen, readers judged pro-Castro writers as much more pro-Castro, as you'd expect. But even when the side was assigned, readers still judged the pro-Castro writers as more pro-Castro than the anti-Castro writers.

That's the fundamental attribution error (a term coined by Lee Ross in 1977): we explain other people's behaviour by their personality and underestimate the situation pushing on them. One main reason is that the person is in plain view, while the pressure on them is invisible to us (Gilbert & Malone, 1995).

Our examples are jokes, not data: the driver who cuts you off, the coworker who misses a deadline, the waiter who forgets your fries. The "you cut someone off? You're late" twist is the related actor-observer bias (Jones & Nisbett, 1971), used here as everyday colour.

How to catch it: when someone annoys you, name one outside reason before you name a flaw.

videos.title: Would You Wear This Sign? You Think Everyone Agrees | Blind Spot #33
videos.description:
Would you walk around campus wearing a giant sign that says "Eat at Joe's"? Whatever you answered, you probably think most people would answer the same.

In 1977, Lee Ross, David Greene and Pamela House at Stanford asked students to do exactly that: wear a sandwich board for 30 minutes, one sign on the chest and one on the back. They were free to refuse. About half said yes and half said no. Then everyone was asked to guess what other students would do. Those who agreed estimated that about 62% of their peers would agree too. Those who refused estimated that only about a third would agree, so about two in three would refuse, like them. Same campus, same sign, two different "everybodies".

That's the false consensus effect: we treat our own choice as the common one. Your brain asks one person, you, and calls it a poll. A later meta-analysis of 115 hypothesis tests (Mullen and colleagues, 1985) found the effect across many topics and groups.

Our examples are jokes, not data: the friend who's sure everyone hates pineapple pizza, the coworker who thinks the whole team wants a weekend retreat, the group chat that feels like the whole country.

How to catch it: before you say "everyone", count the people you actually asked. Then ask someone who disagrees.

videos.title: Ben Franklin's Sneaky Trick to Turn an Enemy Into a Friend | Blind Spot #29
videos.description:
How do you turn an enemy into a friend? Don't do him a favor. Make him do you one.

Philadelphia, the 1730s. Ben Franklin, the guy on the hundred-dollar bill, had a rival: a rich new lawmaker who gave a speech against him. Franklin didn't flatter him. He asked to borrow a rare book from his library. The man sent it right away, Franklin returned it a week later with a thank-you note, and the two stayed friends for life.

In 1969, psychologists Jecker and Landy tested the idea. Students won money in a quiz. Some were then asked by the researcher himself to give it back, as a personal favor. Those students liked him the most.

That's the Ben Franklin effect: when you help someone, your brain asks "why would I do this unless I like them?" and nudges your feelings to match your actions. It's why you love the friend you helped move (twice), root for the new kid you trained, and feel the neighbor's plant you watered is a little bit yours.

How to use it: need an ally? Ask for something small. Borrow the book. Keep the friend.

Note: the 1969 study was small and old, and the effect is an explanation of behavior (reducing the clash between "I helped" and "I don't like them"), not a guarantee. Ask small, say thank you, and don't overdo it.

videos.title: Why Waiters Forget Your Order the Second You Pay | Blind Spot #28
videos.description:
Why can a waiter remember your whole order, then forget it the second you pay?

The story goes: in the 1920s, psychologist Kurt Lewin sat in a café with his students and noticed that the waiter kept the unpaid orders in his head. Once the bill was paid, they were gone. (The anecdote is retold second-hand, so treat it as a story, not a measurement.)

His student Bluma Zeigarnik took the idea to the lab. She gave people quick little tasks: puzzles, beads on a string, clay shapes. Then she stopped some of them halfway. Later she asked what they remembered. In her 1927 data, the interrupted tasks were recalled about twice as often as the finished ones.

That's the Zeigarnik effect: an unfinished job leaves a little alarm ringing in your head, and finishing it shuts the alarm off.

Fair warning: the memory part is shaky. Many later studies could not repeat it, and a 2025 meta-analysis found no overall memory advantage for unfinished tasks. Replications are mixed. What does hold up is the urge to go back and finish an interrupted task. It's why a cliffhanger makes you hit "next episode", why a half-done chore bugs you at 2 a.m., and why "we need to talk" with no follow-up ruins your whole day.

How to catch it: can't sleep over something unfinished? Write down your next step. In one well-known study, making a specific plan stopped the unfinished goal from nagging at people. (That is one study, so treat it as a handy habit, not a guarantee.)

videos.title: How Many Circles Does It Take to Draw a Heart? | Blind Spot M12
videos.description:
A pen on a spinning circle draws... a circle. Put a smaller circle on its edge, spin that too, and keep going. How many circles does it take to draw a perfect heart? Three? Eight? A thousand? For this classic heart: exactly eight, each with its own size and speed. Then we try a star: corners are hard for circles, so we add more. Ten, fifty, two hundred. The corners get sharper every time.

That is a Fourier series. In 1807 Joseph Fourier claimed that any wavy line is just simple waves added up, and a simple wave is a spinning circle seen from the side. The big names in Paris were not convinced. He was right. Your phone shrinks songs and photos with a cousin of this trick. How to catch it: our brain thinks circles can only make round things, so a rule that looks too simple is worth a second look.

How the video was made: the heart is x = 16 sin^3 t, y = 13 cos t - 5 cos 2t - 2 cos 3t - cos 4t. Rewritten as turning circles it needs exactly eight (radii 12.5, 3, 2.5, 2.5, 1, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, speeds 1 to 4 turns per loop, each speed once clockwise and once counter-clockwise). The star is a regular five-point star, transformed numerically; the 10, 50 and 200 biggest circles are drawn. With a finite number of circles only special curves like the heart are exact; a sharp-cornered star needs endlessly many. Everything is our own animation: no real portraits, logos or app names.

videos.title: People Chose MORE Pain. Here's Why Your Memory Lies | Blind Spot #27
videos.description:
Would you ever pick more pain over less? Of course not. Science disagrees.

In 1993, Daniel Kahneman and his colleagues asked people to dip a hand in painfully cold water, twice. The short trial: 60 seconds. The long trial: the same 60 seconds, then 30 more while the water warmed up just a little. Still cold, just less cold. Then they were told they'd do one more trial and could pick which one to repeat. A clear majority chose the long one. Thirty extra seconds of pain, on purpose.

That's the peak-end rule: your memory doesn't add up every second. It keeps two snapshots, the worst moment and the last one, and mostly ignores the time in between (Kahneman calls that duration neglect). It's why a so-so trip with a perfect last day feels amazing, why a great date with an awkward goodbye feels like a disaster, and why one rude waiter at dessert can ruin a whole restaurant.

How to catch it: before you judge something, replay the middle, not just the ending. Hosting a party? Ending a date? Finish strong.

videos.title: One Checkbox Split Germany and Austria | Blind Spot #26
videos.description:
What decides if you'll be an organ donor? Not your values. A little checkbox.

In 2003, psychologists Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein compared countries that handle organ-donor sign-up in two different ways. In Germany you are not a donor unless you sign up. In Austria you are a donor unless you say no. Two neighbours, same language, same mountains.

The result, in terms of consent rates (the share of people counted as willing donors under each rule): about 12% in Germany, 99.98% in Austria. Austrians were not simply nicer. The box was already ticked.

That's the default effect: whatever is already picked for you tends to stay picked. Your brain reads "already set" as "probably fine", and changing it feels like homework. It's why you still pay for an app you opened once, keep the factory ringtone, and have had the same haircut since sixth grade.

How to catch it: once a month, pick one thing you never chose (a plan, a setting, a subscription) and ask: "If this were blank today, would I pick it?"

Note: these are early-2000s consent figures, not the number of transplants actually performed. Real donation rates differ much less, because doctors and families also have a say.

videos.title: Why Spilling Coffee Made a Genius More Likeable | Blind Spot #25
videos.description:
Want people to like you more? Try spilling coffee on yourself.

In 1966, psychologist Elliot Aronson's team played students a tape of a guy trying out for a college quiz team. In one version he was a genius: 92% of the questions right, honor student, yearbook editor, track team. In the other he was average: 30% right. At the end of the tape came a crash, a clatter, and "Oh my goodness, I've spilled coffee all over my new suit."

Then the students rated how much they liked him. The genius who spilled was liked the most, more than the perfect one. The average guy who spilled was liked the least.

That's the pratfall effect: a small slip makes a capable person feel human and closer. The teacher who laughs when the projector dies. The singer who trips and keeps going. The date who spills a drink and laughs. But it only works if you're good first: the coffee only helps the genius.

How to catch it: notice when you hide a small mistake. Don't. Laugh, fix it, move on.

videos.title: Add 1 Meter to a Rope Around Earth. How High? | Blind Spot M11
videos.description:
Wrap a rope tight around the Earth, along the equator: forty thousand kilometers. Now add one meter and lift the rope evenly, all the way around. How high does it float? A hair? A cat? A door? It floats about 16 centimeters up, so a cat could crawl under it from Brazil to Indonesia.

Why? The distance around any circle is 2 x pi times the distance to its center. So one extra meter of rope raises it by 1 m / (2 x pi) = 15.9 cm. The Earth's size never enters the math: a basketball, the Moon and the Sun all get the same 16 cm. Math has no VIP section. How to catch it: when a number is huge, ask if it even matters.

How the video was made: the gap is exactly 1 m / 2 pi = 0.159155 m. In the whole-planet shots the gap is drawn bigger than life and labelled "gap not to scale"; the ground close-up (7 px per cm) and the basketball (ring radius 27.8 cm around a ball of radius 11.9 cm) are drawn to scale. The globe is a stylised drawing with no real coastlines.

videos.title: Why a Tiny Yes Turns Into a Giant Ugly Sign | Blind Spot #23
videos.description:
In 1966, researchers knocked on doors in California and asked people to put a small "Be a safe driver" sign in their window. Most said sure. Two weeks later, someone new came back and asked to put a giant, ugly "Drive Carefully" sign on their front lawn. Only about 1 in 6 people asked cold said yes. Among homes first asked for the tiny sign, about 3 in 4 agreed. Same sign. Same ask.

That's the foot-in-the-door technique: once you've said yes to something small, the next yes feels easier, because you now see yourself as "a person who helps". Saying no starts to feel out of character. It's the pen that becomes twenty bucks, the free trial that becomes a yearly plan, the "just one coffee" that ends with meeting their parents.

How to catch it: when the big ask comes, pretend it came first. Would you say yes out of nowhere?

videos.title: Why Does Pure Luck Always Draw the Same Hill? | Blind Spot M10
videos.description:
Drop a ball through a field of pegs. At every peg it goes left or right, pure luck. Now drop 4,096 of them. Do they pile up flat, on the sides, or in the middle? Every time, they build a hill in the middle: the bell curve.

Why? To hit the far edge, a ball must go right twelve times in a row, and there is exactly one path for that. To land in the exact middle, it can take any mix of six lefts and six rights, and there are very many such paths. Luck piles up where the paths pile up. Francis Galton showed a board like this in 1874 and said the Greeks would have made the law a god. Heights come close to a bell, ten dice added up make the same hill, and many tests are scaled into one on purpose. One ball tells you nothing; a crowd is law.

How the video was made: every ball makes 12 fair coin flips (seeded random numbers), and the pile is just the sum of 4,096 balls, nothing hand-shaped. The final counts per slot were 1, 11, 55, 211, 541, 786, 929, 783, 480, 212, 75, 11, 1. The magenta outline is the exact expectation (1, 12, 66, 220, 495, 792, 924, 792, 495, 220, 66, 12, 1). The ten-dice bars use the exact distribution of the sum of ten dice. The faceless figures are generic drawings.

Last answer (from M9, two blocks and pi): ten clacks. Pi needs a hundred, ten thousand, a million.

videos.title: Why Your Stuff Feels Worth Double (The Mug Test) | Blind Spot #18
videos.description:
In 1990, researchers at Cornell University put a coffee mug on every other desk. Pure luck who got one. Then mug owners could sell and everyone else could buy. Same mug, same room, owned for a few minutes. The result? Sellers asked about twice what buyers would pay, for a mug they had just got for free.

That's the endowment effect: once something is yours, giving it up feels like a loss, and your brain hates losing. The ex's hoodie, the old car, the garage-sale junk that's suddenly "vintage". The mug didn't change. You did.

(The effect is debated: some later studies with very careful instructions and practice rounds found a much smaller gap. The 1990 mug experiment is told here as it was documented.)

Next: #19, follow so you don't miss it
