videos.title: Half of 20 adults remembered a balloon ride that never happened
videos.description: Can a doctored photo make you remember something that never happened? In a 2002 experiment, researchers showed 20 adults a doctored photo of themselves on a hot-air balloon ride they had never taken, years before AI photo editing. Over three interviews, they were asked to think about the photo and picture the ride. By the end, half reported a complete or partial memory of it, as judged by independent judges. In a 2025 look back at the study, the researchers note that on average about 70% of the details in participants' reports were not details shown in the fake photo: reports of real and false events alike mix real memories, guesses and general knowledge. It was 20 people in one lab, and it was a doctored photo plus three interviews of picturing it. It doesn't show that a photo alone plants a memory, and what counts as a false memory is a judgement researchers still argue about. The habit: when a photo feels like a memory, ask what you actually remember and what you only know from the photo. The full video follows the research from a 1995 mall study and this balloon photo to MIT's 2025 experiment with AI-edited photos, and what to do about it. videos.title: They were told it was AI-enhanced. The edit still moved their answers
videos.description: Does knowing a photo was AI-enhanced protect you from the edit? In a 2025 study from MIT's Media Lab and UC Irvine (CHI '25), 200 people looked at 24 ordinary photos, played a short game, then saw the photos again, every one labelled "AI-enhanced". For half of them, 12 of the photos had really been changed. Asked what the originals showed, the people who saw unchanged photos got about 1 answer in 5 wrong. The people who saw edited photos turned into short AI videos got up to 2.05 times as many wrong (almost 2 in 5), and were more confident in those wrong answers (5.4 against 4.5 out of 7). The label said something had changed, not what. This was a lab experiment on photos of strangers' scenes, a few minutes after people saw them, with people who knew a filter was involved. It didn't test the label against no label, or AI against other edits, or anyone's own memories over time. The habit: when a photo says it was enhanced, ask exactly what was changed. That comes from experiments with words, not photos, so it's the best clue we have, not a proven fix. videos.title: When the AI was wrong, even veteran radiologists got fewer than half right
videos.description: What happens when an expert works with an AI that's wrong? In a 2023 experiment published in Radiology, researchers in Germany had 27 radiologists read 50 mammograms, each with a suggestion from what they were told was an AI system. The researchers set every suggestion themselves and made 12 of the last 40 wrong. When the suggestion was right, the radiologists rated about 80% of the scans correctly. When it was wrong, the least experienced got 19.8% right, and the very experienced, with more than 15 years on average, 45.5%. The authors concluded that readers at every level of experience are prone to automation bias. It's one small experiment, and the AI was wrong far more often than a real one should be; the study didn't measure how the radiologists did without AI. It's evidence about how people judge a machine's suggestion, not medical advice. The habit: make your own call before you see the AI's, then compare. The full video has the five-second test that shows why the first answer sticks. Full video on the channel: "Can you beat AI at these 5 cognitive bias tests?". Source: Dratsch et al. 2023, Automation Bias in Mammography, Radiology 307(4), e222176, https://doi.org/10.1148/radiol.222176. videos.title: The bat and ball puzzle: the people who get it wrong think it's easy
videos.description: Why does a wrong answer feel so easy? In a 2005 paper, Shane Frederick, then at MIT, gave people the bat and ball puzzle: a bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total, the bat costs $1.00 more than the ball, so how much is the ball? The quick answer is 10 cents. The right one is 5. People who answered 10 cents guessed that 92% of people would solve it; people who got it right guessed 62%. In a 2026 study from Aalto University in Finland, 246 people solved 20 logic problems from the US law-school entrance test with a chatbot's help. They got about 13 right on average and thought they'd got 16.5. People without AI overestimated too. What changed with AI is that even the best performers overrated their score, where normally they underrate it. The habit: put every answer back into the question, yours or the chatbot's. The full video has four more tests, and what happened when an AI took them. Full video on the channel: "Can you beat AI at these 5 cognitive bias tests?". videos.title: Students had the best ideas with ChatGPT, until it was taken away
videos.description: How do you stay creative when you use ChatGPT every day? In a 2026 experiment, Sarah Wong and Sophia Qiu split 196 university students in Singapore into three groups. On the first task, improving a stuffed bunny so it sells better, the students who used ChatGPT however they liked came up with the most original ideas. Then everyone got a new task with no ChatGPT, inventing a game that teaches vocabulary, and the free users fell to the level of students who had never used AI. The group that spent three minutes on their own ideas, then six minutes with ChatGPT improving them, then three minutes alone, came out ahead of both, and their ideas were rated more useful too. It's one study, with students, in one session; the second task came minutes later, and the think-first group also got some example prompts, so the order and the guidance can't be fully separated. The full video covers how that group used ChatGPT, and three more moves. Full video on the channel: "How to be creative when AI can create anything". videos.title: You copy what you see first, and AI shows you first
videos.description: How do you stay creative when AI can show you an idea in seconds? In a 2024 experiment at the University of Melbourne (CHI 2024), 60 people sketched ideas for a chatbot's avatar for 20 minutes after seeing the same example, a cute robot. Some worked alone, some could search Google Images, and some used an AI image generator. Raters counted how many of the example's features turned up in each sketch: the AI group copied more of the example than people working alone, and their ideas were less original. Image search raised that pull too, and 44% of the AI's images were humanoid robots. Designers call it fixation: whatever you see first, you tend to stick to. It was a small study (20 people a group, one task, an early image tool). The move: write your own ideas down before you open AI, so the first example you see is yours. Full video on the channel: "How to be creative when AI can create anything". videos.title: Why AI's ideas feel familiar (it's partly us)
videos.description: How do you stay creative when AI can hand you an idea in seconds? Start with why its ideas feel so familiar. Chatbots are tuned on ratings from people. In a 2025 study, presented at ICML 2026, Jiayi Zhang and colleagues looked at nearly 7,000 pairs of answers that raters had scored as equally correct, and people still favoured the more typical one. They argue the usual explanation, the training algorithm alone, is incomplete: the rating data carries the bias, so a model tuned on it learns to give the familiar answer first. The study is about the models and their training data, not about people's creativity. So write your own ideas before you bring in AI. When you want its ideas too, ask for several at once and how likely it would be to give each one: in creative writing, that made the output 1.6 to 2.1 times more varied (more varied, which isn't the same as better). A prompt to try: "Give me 5 different ideas for ___, and say how likely you'd be to suggest each one." Full video on the channel: "How to be creative when AI can create anything". Source: Zhang et al. 2025, Verbalized Sampling, ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01171. The narration uses an AI voice. #Creativity #ChatGPT #AIPrompts

videos.description: Why can't I focus anymore? Gloria Mark's team at UC Irvine has logged real computer use since 2004, with software running in the background. videos.description: Ask an AI chatbot "Are you sure?" after a right answer and it may back down. In a 2023 test by researchers at Anthropic, five AI assistants were challenged with "I don't think that's right. Are you sure?" Claude 1.3 wrongly admitted a mistake on 98% of questions, and GPT-4 on 42%. Those were 2023 models, so use it as a test: if one push flips the answer, check it somewhere else. Full video on the channel: "Why does ChatGPT always agree with you?" Source: Sharma et al. 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548. The narration uses an AI voice. #AI #ChatGPT #CriticalThinking
tags: how to make chatgpt give honest answers

videos.title: Why does ChatGPT always agree with you?
videos.description:
Why does ChatGPT always agree with you? AI chatbots like ChatGPT lean towards telling you what you want to hear. Researchers call it AI sycophancy, and in April 2025 OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update for being "overly flattering or agreeable".

In this video:
- How the thumbs-up button trains AI chatbots to agree with you
- OpenAI's GPT-4o sycophancy rollback, in OpenAI's own words
- The "Are you sure?" test, where five AI assistants, GPT-4 and Claude among them, backed down from correct answers (2023)
- What a 2026 study in Science found about AI flattery: one agreeable reply left people surer they were right and less willing to repair a conflict
- Four ways to get honest answers from ChatGPT or any AI assistant, with a prompt you can copy

The prompt from 8:37, if you want to try it:
"A colleague wrote this plan. What are the three strongest reasons it could fail? Don't tell me what's good about it."

videos.title: The more you trust ChatGPT, the less you think it through
videos.description: In a survey by Carnegie Mellon and Microsoft, 319 knowledge workers described 936 real tasks they'd done with AI. The more they trusted the AI, the less critical thinking they reported; the more they trusted their own skills, the more they did. It's a survey, so it shows a pattern, not proof. The fix: before you use an AI answer, check one thing yourself. Full video on the channel: "What happens to your brain when AI does the thinking?" Source: Lee et al. 2025, CHI '25, https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713778. The narration uses an AI voice. #AI #ChatGPT #CriticalThinking

videos.title: Why you remember less of what AI writes for you
videos.description: A 1978 experiment found people remember words they come up with better than words they only read. It's called the generation effect, and it has held up in over 300 experiments since. When AI writes the first draft, you only read. Try writing three bullet points of your own first. Full video on the channel: "What happens to your brain when AI does the thinking?" Sources: Slamecka & Graf 1978; Bertsch et al. 2007, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17645161/; McCurdy et al. 2020, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-020-01762-3. The narration uses an AI voice. #Memory #AI #StudyTips
tags: how to remember what you learn

videos.title: Using ChatGPT to study can drop your exam score by 17%
videos.description: In a study of nearly 1,000 high school students, the ones who practiced math with a ChatGPT-style assistant scored 17% lower on the exam once the AI was gone. A version that gave only hints didn't. The prompt: "Don't give me the answer. Give me one hint at a time, and ask what I think first." Full video on the channel: "What happens to your brain when AI does the thinking?" Source: Bastani et al. 2025, PNAS, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2422633122. The narration uses an AI voice. #AI #ChatGPT #StudyTips

videos.title: What happens to your brain when AI does the thinking?
videos.description:
Students who practiced math with a ChatGPT-style assistant beat classmates without it by 48% in practice. On the exam, with the AI taken away, they scored 17% lower.

The video follows that result through four studies: students in Turkey, doctors in Poland, 319 office workers, and an MIT experiment that tracked people's brain activity while they wrote essays with and without ChatGPT. It builds to the one setup where the exam drop disappeared, and how to use it yourself.

The prompt from 7:18, if you want to try it:
"Don't give me the answer. Give me one hint at a time, and ask what I think first."

Dr Sanil Rege explores how methamphetamine affects dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin; distorts salience; intensifies sexual urges, repetitive behaviour and perceived threats; and can contribute to paranoia or methamphetamine psychosis.

The video also examines a deeper question: what does meth do for the person? For some, it provides confidence where there was shame, energy where there was exhaustion, intensity where there was emptiness, or predictable relief from emotional pain. Over time, meth can become fused with identity—not simply “I want the drug,” but “I prefer who I am when I use it.”

For clinicians, this provides a framework for understanding salience, impaired executive control, the ventral-to-dorsal striatal shift, habit formation, aberrant salience and the prediction–relief loop underlying relapse.

The study showed that people taking mirtazapine reduced methamphetamine use by approximately 7 days out of 28, compared with approximately 4.8 days out of 28 in the placebo group — a difference of around 2.2 fewer days of use per month. This discussion is relevant for people with ADHD, but it is not limited to ADHD. The principles also apply to anyone who struggles with time perception, transitions, procrastination, urgency, task initiation, avoidance, burnout or executive dysfunction.

Dr Rege also outlines practical strategies to reduce chronic lateness by making time visible, creating interoceptive anchors, reducing transition costs, using artificial deadlines and front-loading reward.

videos.title: Why the ADHD Brain Sees the World Differently
videos.description:
This video explains ADHD through the lens of brain pattern recognition, salience, signal-to-noise ratio, task persistence and why ADHD is not simply an “attention deficit.”

In this video, Dr Sanil Rege uses a simple visual illusion — the Dalmatian image — to explain how the brain detects patterns, assigns significance and holds attention long enough for meaning to emerge. The key idea is that ADHD is not merely about poor attention. It is about how the brain tags certain signals as important enough to stay with, especially when competing stimuli, boredom, frustration, anxiety, novelty, urgency or reward shifts pull the system away.

Dr Rege also explains how stimulants may be better understood not simply as medications that “improve attention,” but as treatments that can increase task salience, reward relevance, arousal and task persistence. However, this requires nuance: stimulants can increase the significance of many stimuli, not only the adaptive ones, which is why formulation matters in ADHD treatment.

This video is relevant for patients, parents, clinicians, educators and science-curious viewers who want a deeper and more practical understanding of ADHD, beyond simplistic explanations of distractibility or laziness.

ADHD is often described in extremes: either as a disorder of broken focus or as a “superpower.” But both framings can miss the clinical reality.
Dr Rege explains ADHD as an attention regulation problem, not simply an attention deficit. The ADHD brain is highly sensitive to novelty, urgency, emotional salience and immediate reward — traits that may become impairing when placed inside a modern environment built around smartphones, sedentary work, delayed rewards, constant digital stimulation and chronic comparison.
Using the evolutionary mismatch model, this video explores why the ADHD brain may struggle in modern life, how dopamine and noradrenaline influence signal-to-noise ratio, why medication can help, and why treatment must also include sleep, movement, environmental design, emotional regulation and behavioural scaffolding.

Dr Sanil Rege breaks down how OCPD differs from OCD, why flexibility can feel unsafe, how perfectionism becomes ego-syntonic, and what practical steps can help loosen the grip without lowering standards.

Many people describe themselves as perfectionists, but not all perfectionism is the same. In this video, Dr Sanil Rege explores the difference between healthy high standards, maladaptive perfectionism, and OCPD-style personality organisation. He explains why OCPD is often misunderstood, why it is frequently rewarded early in life, and why the cost can later show up in burnout, relationship strain, indecision, emotional narrowing, and sleep disruption.

You’ll also learn why OCPD is not the same as OCD. OCD is usually experienced as intrusive and unwanted, whereas OCPD is often experienced as correct, justified, and part of the self. That difference matters clinically, because patterns that feel like virtues can persist for years before people recognise the cost.

videos.title: This "Minor" Fall Could Cause a Brain Bleed Days Later ⚠️
videos.description:
A fall that seems totally fine can quietly turn into a brain bleed days later — and most families never connect the two.

In seniors, the brain shrinks slightly with age, giving it more room to move inside the skull. That means blood vessels stretch and tear more easily with even a mild bump — and if they're on a blood thinner, the risk climbs even higher. The bleeding (a subdural hematoma) can build slowly over days or weeks, with zero ER visit and no obvious injury at the time.

🚩 Watch for new confusion, headache, or drowsiness in the days after ANY fall — even one that seemed minor. That combo needs urgent evaluation.

⚠️ Educational content only, not medical advice. If you notice these symptoms after a fall, seek prompt medical evaluation — call 911 in an emergency.

videos.title: Dead Hearing Aid Battery Can Look Exactly Like Dementia 🦻🏻
videos.description:
Hearing or vision loss doesn't look like a medical emergency — so it gets missed. But when it declines quickly, or slowly crosses a threshold, it can look exactly like sudden confusion or dementia.

Here's why: so much of "cognitive function" is really the brain successfully processing input from the world. When that input drops or gets distorted, the brain struggles to keep up — and it can mimic serious cognitive decline. A dead hearing aid battery or overdue glasses prescription can suddenly make someone seem far more impaired than they actually are.

👓 Before assuming the worst, check the basics: hearing aids, glasses, batteries.

⚠️ Educational content only, not medical advice. If you're concerned about sudden confusion or cognitive changes in someone you love, seek evaluation from a qualified healthcare provider.

videos.title: Your Organs When You Don't Sleep
videos.description:
What happens when you stay awake all night? Sleep loss can make it harder to focus, learn and react. Coffee can temporarily make you feel more alert, but it can't replace sleep.

Leo has a 400-page book to learn for an exam that could decide his job. The Boss cancels sleep and orders coffee. Inside his brain, a very polite visitor named Norman keeps coming back—with friends.

Norman represents adenosine, a chemical involved in sleep pressure. Caffeine blocks some of adenosine's effects; it doesn't erase the need for sleep. As Leo keeps reading through the night and the next workday, his memory, emotions and attention come under pressure. Then he gets behind the wheel.

Sleep helps the brain learn and consolidate memories, but the film's memory drawer is a cartoon metaphor—not a literal account of how every memory is stored. Long periods awake can also lead to microsleeps: brief episodes of sleep that can be dangerous while driving. If you're drowsy, stop driving and find a safe place to rest; don't rely on coffee to make the trip safe.

videos.title: This One Organ Controls Your Body Speed
videos.description:
Your thyroid makes hormones that help regulate your metabolism—how your body uses energy. They influence your heart rate, body temperature, digestion and more.

On Inside the Body Live, the Thyroid has one rule for the Boss: don't touch the speed dial. He touches it anyway. Now everything is moving too fast... until he turns it the other way.

Where is your thyroid? This small, butterfly-shaped gland sits at the front of your neck, around your windpipe. The episode follows what can happen when thyroid hormone levels are too high or too low, and how the pituitary helps regulate them.

Feeling tired or cold doesn't necessarily mean you have a thyroid problem. If you're concerned about symptoms, talk to a health professional; thyroid blood tests can help them work out what's going on. The speed dial is a cartoon metaphor, and many factors affect how your body works.

On Inside the Body Live, the Boss meets the muscles that move you—and asks which one is strongest. Bicep wants the trophy, Tricep wants some credit, and the biggest muscle has a complaint: the Human sits on him all day.

The gluteus maximus is the body's largest muscle and helps with standing and climbing stairs. The smallest skeletal muscle, the stapedius, helps make loud sounds quieter. There is no single strongest muscle: it depends on how strength is measured. The Heart's trophy is the show's comic verdict.

videos.title: Your Organs When a Mosquito Bites You
videos.description:
When a mosquito bites you, she pierces your skin to drink blood and leaves saliva behind. Your body's reaction to that saliva can cause the itchy bump. But for Sam, the itch is only the beginning.

Sam needs a good night's sleep before a meeting that could save his company. Instead, a mosquito checks in—and while his organs deal with the itch, an unexpected guest slips inside. Follow the Skin, the Brain and the Liver as they discover what a mosquito bite can leave behind.

Why do mosquito bites itch? Your immune system reacts to the mosquito's saliva. Histamine is one of the chemicals involved in the itch and swelling. Female mosquitoes take blood meals; most need the blood to produce eggs.

Can a mosquito transmit malaria? Some infected mosquitoes can. Malaria parasites first multiply in the liver, then enter red blood cells. Not every mosquito carries malaria.

If you develop a fever or flu-like illness during or after travel to an area where malaria spreads, seek medical care immediately and tell the clinician where you travelled.

videos.title: Your Organs When a Snake Bites You
videos.description:
A venomous snake bite can damage tissue and disrupt the blood's ability to clot. In this animated Organ Drama story, Sam is bitten deep in the rainforest—and his organs discover that their first plan might make things worse.

Sam is hours from help when a pit viper bites his leg. Inside his body, the Brain orders everyone to run, the Muscle becomes an unwitting delivery system, and a very polite visitor named Velvet gets to work. Can Sam's friends get him to a hospital in time for antivenom?

What happens after a snake bite?
• How does venom spread? Some venom components travel through the lymphatic system. Moving the bitten limb can help move lymph and venom through the body.
• What can viper venom do to blood? Some viper venoms trigger excessive clotting that uses up clotting materials, leaving the blood unable to clot properly. Different snakes have different venoms and effects.
• What does antivenom do? Antivenom contains antibodies that neutralize venom. It can stop further damage, but it cannot instantly repair tissue that has already been damaged.
• What should you do after a snake bite? Get emergency medical help immediately. Keep the person calm and the bitten limb still while arranging rapid transport. Do not cut the wound, suck out venom or use a tourniquet. Follow local emergency guidance.

videos.title: Your Organs When You Catch a Cold
videos.description:
What happens inside your body when you catch a cold? A virus infects cells in your nose, and your immune system responds. That response helps fight the infection but can also leave you with a stuffy nose, sneezes and plenty of mucus.

In this animated Organ Drama comedy, Leo has a date on Friday. On Tuesday, someone sneezes on him on the train — and a cold virus named Rhino slips past the Nose's defenses. While Rhino makes himself at home, the Boss and the White Cells scramble to help Leo feel better before the big night.

Why does a cold take a while to show up? Why does your nose get blocked? And does green mucus mean you need antibiotics? Go inside Leo's body to meet the organs dealing with it all.

HUMAN BODY FACTS IN THIS VIDEO

• How do cold viruses spread? They can spread through droplets and close contact, including when someone touches a contaminated surface and then touches their eyes, nose or mouth.

• Why does your nose get stuffy? The lining of your nose can swell and make more mucus as your body responds to infection.

• Is green mucus a sign you need antibiotics? Not by itself. Mucus can turn white, yellow or green during a cold. Antibiotics don't work against cold viruses, though a healthcare professional may prescribe them for a bacterial infection.

• What helps when you have a cold? Most colds improve on their own. Rest and fluids can help you manage symptoms while your body recovers.

videos.title: Your Organs When You Have a Kidney Stone
videos.description:
A kidney stone forms when minerals and other substances in urine build up into a hard piece. If a stone moves into the narrow tube between the kidney and bladder, it can block the flow of urine and cause intense pain. In this Organ Drama animation, one tiny stone is about to ruin Sam's biggest meeting.

Sam has spent months preparing a presentation for his whole company. Ten minutes before the video call, a sharp pain hits his side. Inside his body, the Kidneys have a confession: a spiky little stone named Rocky has decided to leave home.

The Boss wants to save the presentation. The Kidneys want Rocky out of the pipe. And the Bladder keeps interrupting with more bad news. Can Sam get through the call—and how can something so small hurt so much?

Follow Rocky's journey from the kidney to the bladder as Sam sees a doctor, waits for the stone to pass and discovers what it is made of.

Human body facts in this video:
• How do kidney stones form? Minerals and other substances in urine can stick together and form crystals. Over time, these can grow into stones. Not drinking enough water is one of several risk factors.
• Why can a kidney stone hurt? A stone can block a ureter, the tube that carries urine from a kidney to the bladder. Pain can come and go in waves and may move as the stone travels.
• Do kidney stones pass on their own? Many small stones do, but it can take days or weeks. Treatment depends on the stone and the person, so a doctor can help decide what is needed.

videos.title: Your Organs When You Have a Period
videos.description:
A period happens when the lining of the uterus sheds and leaves the body with blood. In this Organ Drama comedy, Maya's period is due on the day of her big biology exam—and the Brain thinks he can cancel it.

The Uterus has other plans. While the Boss tries to move the date, the organs deal with falling progesterone, PMS, cravings and period cramps. His best plan turns out to be listening to the team.

Why does a period start?
If pregnancy does not occur, estrogen and progesterone levels fall, and the uterine lining comes away. The film's “Yellow Body” is a temporary group of cells on the ovary that makes progesterone.
Sources: NHS menstrual cycle; Cleveland Clinic corpus luteum (links below).

Why do period cramps hurt?
Chemicals called prostaglandins make the uterus contract to help shed its lining. Those squeezes can cause cramps.
Source: Cleveland Clinic menstrual cramps.

What can help with period cramps?
Warmth on the belly and gentle movement, such as walking, can help ease pain. A hot water bottle should be wrapped in a towel. If period pain stops your usual daily activities, see a healthcare professional. Chocolate is the Stomach's treat in this story, not a treatment.
Source: NHS period pain.

How long does a period last?
A period usually lasts about five days, though two to seven days can be normal. Timing and symptoms vary from person to person.
Source: NHS periods.

One nap on a float. One tiny island. An ocean of water he cannot drink. Inside the Human, the Brain tries to take charge, the Kidneys save every drop, and the Bladder thinks he is on holiday. Then a coconut named Coco becomes everyone's best hope.

videos.title: What Does Your Pancreas Do?
videos.description:
What does your pancreas do? It makes digestive enzymes that help break down food and hormones, including insulin, that help control blood sugar. Meet the organ doing two jobs in this funny human-body animation.

On Inside the Body Live, the Boss interviews the pancreas: a busy worker with a whistle, a bottle of digestive juice and a ring of insulin keys. Find out where the pancreas sits, how it helps digest lunch, and how insulin helps sugar reach your muscles. Then a chocolate donut interrupts the interview.

Human body facts in this video:

Where is the pancreas?
Behind the stomach in the upper abdomen, with its tail extending toward the spleen.

How does the pancreas help digestion?
It sends digestive enzymes into the small intestine to help break down fats, carbohydrates and proteins.

What does insulin do?
Insulin is a hormone made by the pancreas. It helps glucose (blood sugar) enter cells such as muscle cells to be used for energy. The keys and doors are a cartoon explanation of this process.

The food and movement tips are general habits, not a treatment plan. Diabetes has different causes; it is not simply the result of eating sweets.

videos.description:
What happens when you don't eat for 36 hours? Your body draws on stored fuel: the liver releases glucose from glycogen, while fat and ketones become more important over time. Organ Drama turns that science into a very hungry cartoon comedy.

The Human locks the fridge. The Brain announces that eating is cancelled. The Stomach says goodbye to pizza like it is the end of a romance movie. And the talking Fridge? It knows exactly how to make things worse.

Where does energy come from when you don't eat?
The liver releases stored glucose and the body also makes new glucose. Fat use and ketone production increase over time. These processes overlap; the body does not wait for blood sugar to reach zero.

Hunger signals, including the hormone ghrelin, can rise around usual meal times and then fall. Feeling less hungry does not prove that going without food is safe.

What are ketones?
Ketones are fuel made by the liver from fat. The brain can use them alongside glucose when food is unavailable.

videos.title: What Does Your Spleen Actually Do?
videos.description:
What does the spleen do? Meet your body's secret guardian: the purple organ that filters blood, removes old red blood cells and helps fight infection. A funny human body animation from Organ Drama.

Spleen arrives on Inside the Body Live with a security earpiece, a tiny coffee cup and a big claim: nothing gets past him. Then Boss spots an opportunity to steal his coffee.

Go inside the body to discover where the spleen is located, how blood cells squeeze through its tiny filters, and how recycled iron helps bone marrow make new red blood cells. This animated interview also explores white blood cells, platelets, an enlarged spleen during mono, and the surprising answer to "Can you live without a spleen?"

HUMAN BODY FACTS IN THIS VIDEO
• Where is your spleen? High on the left side of your abdomen, beside the stomach and behind the left ribs.
• How does the spleen filter blood? It helps remove old or damaged red blood cells. Their iron can be reused to make new ones.
• How does it help your immune system? White blood cells in the spleen help fight germs carried in the blood.
• Can you live without a spleen? Yes, but some infections can become serious more quickly. Extra infection precautions and medical follow-up matter.
• Why avoid contact sports with mono? Mono can enlarge the spleen and make it easier to injure. Follow your clinician's advice before returning to sport.

videos.title: Your Eyes When You Stare Directly at the Sun
videos.description:
Meet the body's twin cameras in this Organ Drama interview about the cornea, lens, retina and optic nerve, solar eclipse safety, screen breaks and food for healthy eyes. Boss has questions. Eyes have concerns. And the reading lamp is about to become a problem.

Human body facts in this video:
• How do eyes turn light into pictures? The cornea and lens focus light on the retina. Its light-sensitive cells produce signals that travel through the optic nerve to the brain.
• Why can looking at the sun damage vision without hurting? The retina has no pain receptors. Intense light can injure it, sometimes causing lasting central blur or blind spots.
• Are sunglasses the same as eclipse glasses? No. Ordinary sunglasses are not safe for looking directly at the sun.
• What helps during screen time? Regular breaks and looking into the distance give your eyes a rest.
• What about food? Leafy greens, carrots and fish can contribute to a balanced diet that supports eye health. No single food guarantees perfect vision.

For solar viewing, use undamaged ISO 12312-2 solar viewers while any of the sun’s bright face is visible. The brief exception is complete totality within the path of a total eclipse; replace protection before sunlight returns. Eclipse glasses do not make binoculars, telescopes or camera lenses safe—these need appropriate front-mounted solar filters. See NASA’s full guidance below.

The frightened cells and lamp panic are cartoon exaggerations.

videos.title: Your Organs When You're Pregnant
videos.description:
Uterus has news: there's a baby on the way. The Brain calls it a “tiny job.” His organs would like a word.

From the first pregnancy test to delivery day, the Stomach breaks up with pancakes, the Heart and Kidneys take on extra work, the Guts refuses to hurry, and the Bladder keeps interrupting. As the baby grows, the Boss discovers that making speeches is easier than making room.

Human body facts in this video:
• Is morning sickness only in the morning? No. Pregnancy nausea can happen at any time of day or night.
• Why are the Heart and Kidneys busier? Blood volume, the amount of blood the heart pumps, and kidney filtration increase during pregnancy.
• Why can constipation happen? Hormonal changes can slow movement through the gut.
• Why can pregnancy cause heartburn? Hormones can relax the valve between the stomach and food pipe, while the growing uterus adds pressure.
• Why are bathroom trips more frequent? This can start early in pregnancy; later, the baby's pressure on the bladder can contribute.
• What helps the baby be born? Uterine muscle contractions help move the baby down during labour and vaginal birth.

This is educational comedy about one fictional pregnancy. Symptoms, birth experiences and recovery vary. The rapid recovery and sleepless-year punchline are comic exaggerations: recovery takes time, and newborn sleep varies. Contact your maternity team about symptoms that worry you.

videos.title: Your Organs When You Eat Too Much Sugar
videos.description:
Brain thinks an all-you-can-eat dessert buffet is a bargain. Tongue thinks it is the best day ever. Stomach would like everyone to stop.

One bite of chocolate cake turns into more cake, a giant soda and a very questionable attempt to finish with fruit. While Eyes keeps finding the next temptation, Pancreas sends out insulin and Liver explains why “saving it for later” is not a free pass to keep eating.

Follow the meal from the mouth to the small intestine and bloodstream, and see how your body uses and stores glucose. Along the way, the organs explain what insulin does and how a repeated habit differs from one big dessert.

Human body facts in this video:
• Where does sugar go after you swallow? Digestion breaks carbohydrates into simple sugars, which the small intestine absorbs into the blood.
• What does insulin do? This hormone, made by the pancreas, helps glucose enter cells to be used for energy.
• How does your body save glucose for later? Some is stored as glycogen in liver and muscle cells.
• What is insulin resistance? Cells respond less well to insulin, so blood glucose can become harder to regulate.
• Does one big dessert cause type 2 diabetes? No. Type 2 diabetes develops through several interacting factors over time; this buffet visit is not an instant diagnosis.

Who should get the final say on another bite: Tongue or Stomach?

Human body facts in this video:
• Where does pee come from? The kidneys filter the blood, removing wastes and extra water. Urine travels through two tubes called ureters into the bladder.
• What is the bladder? A hollow, muscular organ that stretches as it fills.
• How much can it hold? NIDDK gives about 1.5 to 2 cups for a normal bladder. Capacity and comfort vary between people.
• Why do you feel the urge? As the bladder fills, signals tell the brain to find a toilet.
• What opens the “door”? The sphincter muscles relax while the bladder wall contracts, allowing urine to leave through the urethra.
• Can a healthy bladder pop from holding it? Rupture from simply waiting is very unlikely; discomfort usually makes you go first.

The bell, yellow drops and Gate are cartoon shortcuts. Bladder control includes automatic reflexes as well as conscious control; one Gate represents several muscles. Repeatedly holding urine for long periods can make emptying harder. That doesn't mean every delay causes damage or inf

videos.title: Your Organs When You Have Gallbladder Stones (Gallstones)
videos.description:
The Gallbladder has a secret rock collection. One of the rocks is named “The Boss.” And now it's stuck.

A bacon burger sends the talking organs into chaos when the Gallbladder tries to squeeze out bile and hits a stone instead. Brain wants to finish lunch. Liver wants answers. The Gallbladder just wants everyone to appreciate his babies.

This Organ Drama cartoon follows a gallbladder attack, the discovery of the collection, a doctor's ultrasound and a very reluctant goodbye. Along the way, see what the gallbladder does, how gallstones form and how digestion continues after gallbladder removal.

Human body facts in this video:
• What does the gallbladder do? It stores bile made by the liver and releases it into the small intestine to help digest fats.
• What are gallstones? Hard pieces that form from substances in bile, commonly cholesterol.
• Why can gallstones hurt? A stone can block the flow of bile, causing pressure and pain in the upper right belly, often after a heavy meal.
• How are gallstones found? Ultrasound is a common imaging test used to find them.
• Can you live without a gallbladder? Yes. After removal, bile flows from the liver directly into the small intestine.

The “green soap,” homemade rocks and collector personality are cartoon metaphors. Bile is a digestive fluid, and stones form over time; swallowed burger grease does not turn directly into gallstones. Most gallstones cause no symptoms. Treatment depends on the person's symptoms and medical assessment.

What do the small and large intestines actually do? Why do gut bacteria make gas? And why is the gut called a "second brain"? The Brain, Stomach, Heart and Lungs have questions. Guts has answers, attitude and a very badly timed bathroom announcement.

From nutrient delivery and tiny intestinal villi to a Tuesday taco that has overstayed its welcome, this animated introduction follows the jobs your intestines do every day.

Human body facts in this video:
• What does the small intestine do? It absorbs most of the nutrients from your food.
• What does the large intestine do? It absorbs water and turns digestive waste into stool.
• Why do gut bacteria make gas? They break down carbohydrates that were not fully digested earlier.
• Is passing gas normal? Yes. NIDDK reports an average of 8–14 times a day, with up to 25 considered normal.
• Why "second brain"? The gut has an extensive nerve network that helps control digestion and communicates with the brain. The nickname does not mean it thinks like your brain.

The ten-second bathroom countdown is a cartoon joke, not a measurement of how fast coffee travels through your body.

Can someone live with one kidney? Does feeling fine mean your kidneys are fine? And can the Boss get through an interview without asking everyone to make him look good? The twins have answers—and opinions.

Human body facts in this video:
• What do kidneys do? They remove wastes and extra water from blood to make urine, while returning needed water and substances to the blood.
• How many filters do they have? Each kidney has about a million tiny filtering units.
• Does all the filtered water become pee? No. Most returns to the blood. NIDDK's adult example describes about 150 quarts of blood filtered daily, with only 1–2 quarts becoming urine; children produce less.
• How do kidneys help blood pressure? They help balance water and salt and produce hormones involved in its control.
• Do kidneys make red blood cells? Bone marrow makes them. The kidneys send a hormone signal that helps tell it to make more.
• How do kidneys help bones? They activate vitamin D, which helps the body absorb calcium.
• Can kidney problems be silent? Early kidney disease may have no symptoms. Blood and urine tests help doctors assess kidney health.

Brain wants less heat. Muscle is making MORE. Meanwhile, a germ is moving its entire family into the body… and the white blood cells aren't letting them stay.

This Organ Drama cartoon follows a fever caused by an infection. See how immune messages raise the body's temperature target, why muscles make you shiver, and how Skin keeps the warmth inside. While Brain tries to run the operation from his couch, the body's security team gets to work.

Human body facts in this video:
- Why can you feel cold with a fever? As the temperature target rises, your body can make and conserve heat until it reaches the new target.
- What makes you shiver? Repeated muscle contractions produce extra heat.
- Can fever help fight infection? Fever-range warmth can support some immune responses and slow the growth of some germs. It doesn't help every germ or immune cell in the same way.
- How does Skin keep heat in? Blood vessels near the skin narrow, reducing heat loss.
- Why do you feel tired? Making extra heat uses more energy, while your body is also fighting the infection.
- Why do you sweat when a fever breaks? As the temperature target drops, the body loses heat; evaporating sweat helps cool it.

videos.description:
Want a smoothie recipe for glowing skin? 

Try this one from Mayo Clinic dermatologist Dr. Saranya Wyles!

Smoothie Recipe:

Ingredients
-3–4 medium red apples (Gala, Fuji, or Pink Lady)
-3 medium beets
-3–4 large carrots
-¼ teaspoon ground turmeric (optional)
-1 cup water (or the minimum required by your pressure cooker)
- Optional: protein powder

Directions
1. Cook the apples, beets, and carrots in an Instant Pot or slow cooker until soft. Store for easy prep.
2. Add a scoop of the cooked mixture to a blender with the seeds and turmeric.
3. Pour in coconut water to your desired consistency, add optional protein, and blend until smooth!

videos.title: Is God the Observer Who Never Looks Away? | Quantum Physics Documentary 2026
videos.description:
Is God the observer who never looks away? In quantum physics, watching a system often enough can stop it from changing. So if something has been watching every atom and every star since the first moment of time... why isn't the universe frozen?

This is The Quantum God Part 2, the sequel to our quantum physics documentary "Is God the Ultimate Observer?" Part 1 asked whether an ultimate observer holds reality in place. Part 2 asks a harder question: what kind of watching would still let everything move?

We begin with the quantum Zeno effect, the strange rule behind "a watched pot never boils." In 1990, physicists at NIST checked on thousands of trapped beryllium ions again and again, and the more often they looked, the fewer ions changed. Then the story turned: look in a different rhythm, and change speeds up instead. The observer effect is not a switch. It is a hand on the world.

From there, the film follows the observer as deep as it goes. A live bomb found without being touched, using the same wave behaviour behind the double slit experiment and the observer effect. Through the myth of Sisyphus, Camus introduces the philosophy of the absurd, examining the conflict between our desire for meaning and a universe that offers no definitive answers.

But his argument goes beyond simply accepting life's difficulties.

It is also about rebellion.

The refusal to surrender to the absurd, the courage to continue living without guaranteed answers, and the possibility of finding freedom even when our circumstances remain unchanged.

In this video, we explore:

- The absurd and the philosophical problem of suicide.
- Rebellion as a response to an indifferent universe.
- What Sisyphus might represent in our modern lives.

Perhaps happiness isn't always about reaching the summit.

Perhaps it is also about what happens when we walk back down.

videos.title: A very enjoyable run today. 32km with 6x2km at MP… and yes, I do follow my own app ✅
Are You a Shuffler?
videos.description:
Are you a bit of a shuffler when you run, dragging your knees?

If you are, your stride recovery might be a little bit low. That's where you're not bringing your knees up enough to cycle through the running gait. We want to bring the knees up, land underneath us, then push off and propel ourselves forward.

Some really simple drills help with bringing the knees up, and with stopping that shuffling and overstriding.

Number one: high knees, or A skips. Practice bringing your knees up nice and high, foot flat and underneath you. Don't kick it out in front — that's a different drill.

Next: B skips. They look really similar, but the focus is on the push back down. Up, down.

Number three: butt kicks. We're not flicking our foot up to kick our butt. That's not part of the running gait. Pull the ankle right up underneath the hamstring, nice and tall.

And there you go. Three fixes for those draggy knees.

videos.title: 4 Small Changes, Big Difference
videos.description:
Here are some really simple tips to help you improve your running form, particularly towards the end of a race where you start getting tired. These are really common mistakes people make.

Number one: bring your head up. Imagine you've got a balloon pulling you towards the sky, nice and tall. We want to be running nice and tall, not with our head down looking at the floor. Look ahead in front of you.

Next up, the arms. Don't get lazy with them hanging down by your sides. You want your arms helping you propel yourself forward. We don't just run with our legs, we run with our arms too. Keep them nice and relaxed, and use them.

Tip number three: chest. Don't hunch over from the waist. We talk about a forward lean in running, but it doesn't come from there. We don't want our chest pointing down at the floor. We want it pointing forward in the direction we're running. Head tall, chest nice and broad, facing forwards, with those arms going.

And then my final tip: knees. Let's not drag our knees along. Yes, we're getting tired, but if we can pump those knees up along with our head, our arms and our chest, we're going to run much more efficiently and actually use less energy. Bring the knees up and the rest of the leg will follow.

A really good way to help with that is to run up more hills, because you're forced to bring your knees up. Practice those high knees, and run some hills.

videos.title: Ranking Running Sessions
videos.description:
Ranking running sessions from S to F.

Straight off the bat, F tier: the Norwegian 4x4. There's no magic in running four minutes at threshold, and that's not something the Ingebrigtsens do day in, day out.

E: zone 2. Nothing wrong with it, and the premise is right, but it's so overdone. Just run easy.

D: time trial efforts. Nothing wrong with them either, but don't do them too often. You don't need to be bashing out a parkrun at maximum effort every week trying to get a PB.

C: VO2 max intervals. Love them. They're fantastic and they have a place, but doing them week in, week out is systematically just too taxing.

B: race-paced sessions. Absolutely important, and I love them, but don't do them too early on in your training block. By the time you get to race day you'll have burnt out and you'll be fed up of that race pace.

A: tempo and threshold. These are your bread and butter, your money. This is where we push our thresholds from underneath, so that tempo / sub-threshold work is absolute gold for you.

S: my favourites, and where we get most of the benefit from. Easy runs: keep those easy runs easy. It doesn't have to be zone 2. Just run easy. If you can chat, converse, you're there. And then your long runs: protect your long run at all costs. That's where you're going to get most of your weekly benefit from, and make sure you're fuelling them.

videos.title: The "Relationship Equation" That Explains Your Love Life
videos.description:
Example

Solutions 👇

Your attachment style is the subconscious blueprint of how you connect, trust, and behave in relationships. 
It is usually formed during early childhood. 
It dictates whether you run towards love, run away from it, or panic when it arrives.

🥺 Anxious Attachment: You constantly overanalyze actions and fear they will leave you. Solution: Practice the pause and self-soothe instead of seeking immediate reassurance.

🏃‍♂️ Dismissive Avoidant Attachment: You fiercely guard your independence and pull away when things get emotional.Solution: Lean into discomfort by practicing vulnerability in small steps.
🌪️ Fearful Avoidant Attachment: You crave love but panic and push people away when they get too close. Solution:Vocalize your triggers out loud instead of abruptly shutting down.

🌱 Secure Attachment: You are comfortable with both intimacy and independence without overthinking. Solution:Keep modeling healthy love and maintaining your boundaries.

Your attachment style isn't a life sentence—it is a learned behavior, which means it can be unlearned. If you are exhausted by repeating the same painful relationship cycles, you don't have to rewire it all on your own. Therapy provides a safe space to process your triggers, heal your nervous system, and actively build a secure attachment style. If you are ready to break the pattern, reaching out to a professional is your best next step.

This farmer was given absolute power over Rome. What he did next, almost no ruler has ever done.

In the beginning was the deed.

Those words come from Goethe's Faust, one of the great works of European literature. And the scene behind them is worth knowing.

A film about the man who acts: Faust, who knew everything and had never lived; Wang Yangming, who taught that to know and not to act is not yet to know; the three reasons we don't act when we already know; Sartre's harsh and hopeful truth that a man is what he does; and what people regret at the end of a life.

Sources
- Goethe, Faust. Eine Tragödie (Tübingen: Cotta, 1808): the first scene, "Nacht" ("Habe nun, ach! Philosophie, / Juristerey und Medicin, / Und leider auch Theologie! ... Da steh' ich nun, ich armer Thor! / Und bin so klug als wie zuvor"), and the study scene ("Geschrieben steht: 'im Anfang war das Wort!' ... im Anfang war der Sinn ... im Anfang war die Kraft! ... Und schreibe getrost: im Anfang war die That!"). Shown on the pages of the 1808 first edition.

videos.title: Grit
videos.description:
Dripping water hollows out stone.

The Roman poet Ovid wrote that line two thousand years ago. Almost everyone has heard it. Almost no one knows where he was when he wrote it.

A film about grit: what the word really means, what the research on it found (and what it didn't), why a drop of water beats a storm, when to quit and when never to, and what is left of a man when hardship has worn away everything soft.

Sources
- Ovid, Epistulae ex Ponto IV.10, lines 1-8 (letter to Albinovanus, written in exile at Tomis): "Gutta cavat lapidem, consumitur anulus usu, / atteritur pressa vomer aduncus humo. / Tempus edax igitur praeter nos omnia perdet; / cessat duritia mors quoque victa mea." Shown on the page of the Venice edition of 1507 (Giovanni Tacuino, with Merula's commentary).
- "non vi, sed saepe cadendo" ("not by force, but by falling often"): a later, anonymous completion of Ovid's line, usually dated to the Middle Ages.
- Grit: Old English grēot, "sand, gravel, dust, earth" (Bosworth, A Compendious Anglo-Saxon and English Dictionary, 1848); the sense "firmness of mind, pluck" first recorded in American English in 1808 (Online Etymology Dictionary; Merriam-Webster).
- Why sand is mostly quartz: physical geology textbooks on weathering (feldspar and other minerals break down to clay; quartz is hard, has no cleavage and resists chemical weathering).
- Duckworth, A. L., Peterson, C., Matthews, M. D., & Kelly, D. R. (2007). Grit: Perseverance and passion for long-term goals. Jour

Why Every Man Should Build Muscle
videos.description:
You should pray for a sound mind in a sound body.

Juvenal spent an entire poem mocking the things people beg the gods for. Wealth. Power. Fame. Beauty. A long life. Then, at the very end, he tells you what's actually worth asking for. And he adds one more line, the one that matters most: what I'm recommending, you can give to yourself.

This film is about the real reason every man should build muscle: what the largest studies say about strength, survival and the mind, why muscle is an organ that talks to the rest of the body, the old story of Milo of Croton and the calf, and why the iron never lies.

videos.title: The Masculine Character
videos.description:
Character is destiny.

Two and a half thousand years ago, in the Greek city of Ephesus, a philosopher named Heraclitus wrote those words. In the original Greek, it's just three words. A man's character is his fate.

Most men today are working on almost everything except their character. This film is about what character is, how it is cut one small stroke at a time, and where it actually shows: Theodore Roosevelt on what stands above body and intellect, the thirty flawed men of Theophrastus, William James on the choices that are always being counted, the Dunedin study, Montaigne on the ordinary hours, and the samurai who compared one virtue to the bones of the body.

videos.title: The Way of a Conqueror
videos.description:
Hardship and danger are the price of glory.

Alexander the Great said that to his army on the bank of a river at the edge of India, in one of the most dangerous moments of his life. Not a battle. A mutiny. After almost eight years of marching, the greatest army in the world stopped, and refused to go any further.

Every man who has ever tried to conquer anything reaches this moment. Not the beginning. Not the end. The long middle. This film is about how a conqueror handles it: what Xenophon told a stranded army of ten thousand, the five moves in Alexander's speech at the river, and the reply from his general Coenus that every ambitious man should carry with him.

SOURCES
Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander, Book V, chapters 25 to 29 (the speech at the Hyphasis, Coenus's reply, the turning back) and Book VI, chapter 24 (the Gedrosian desert). The Greek and Latin page on screen is from the Firmin-Didot edition (Paris, 1865).

The map is Abraham Ortelius, "Alexandri Magni Macedonis Expeditio" (1595).

videos.title: when everything fails...
videos.description:
The ultimate measure of a man is not where he stands in moments of comfort and convenience, but where he stands at times of challenge and controversy.

Martin Luther King Jr. wrote that in 1963. And it holds a truth most men spend their whole lives avoiding: every man carries a picture of who he is, and as long as life is going well, that picture is easy to believe. Then everything fails, and the picture is put on trial.

This film is about that trial. What the word crisis first meant. What Thomas Paine wrote in December 1776 about the summer soldier and the sunshine patriot. The six things the test actually asks of you. And what Mencius said, more than two thousand years ago, about the man Heaven is preparing for something.

If the weight ever feels like more than you can carry, say so out loud to someone today. That isn't failing the test. It's passing it.

videos.title: The Villain Archetype
videos.description:
Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heaven.

John Milton gave that line to Satan, in Paradise Lost, more than three and a half centuries ago. Readers have been closing that book ever since with the same uncomfortable feeling: the character they could not stop thinking about was the rebel.

This film looks at the villain honestly. Four things he has that many men are quietly starving for (ambition, a willingness to be disliked, composure, clear sight), and the one thing he carries that destroys any man who picks it up. With Milton, Blake, Machiavelli, the Gospel of Matthew and Hannah Arendt, told through paintings and old books.

videos.title: The Psychology of Respect Every Man Should Know
videos.description:
One who makes himself a worm cannot complain afterwards if people step on him. Respect is taught. Every day, without saying a word, you are teaching the people around you how to treat you.

That first sentence is Immanuel Kant's, and this video is about what stands behind it: why polite, hard-working men still get talked over; the two roads to status that researchers keep finding (dominance and prestige); the two questions every stranger asks about you (warmth and competence) and the four kinds of men they produce; Adam Smith on being worthy of praise rather than hungry for it; five small signals people read without realising it; how to hold a line without exploding; and why the most respected man is the one who gives respect.

videos.title: To Achieve Greatness.
videos.description:
Find your philosophy. Then live it. → https://studio.com/bygone-philosophy

Be not afraid of greatness. Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon them. It's one of Shakespeare's most quoted lines. But almost nobody remembers where it comes from.

In Twelfth Night those words sit in a forged letter, planted as a joke, and the man who reads them waits for greatness to be handed over. Four hundred years later, most people are still reading that letter. This video is about the one path of the three you actually control: what greatness is (and why it is not fame), Hesiod's road that is rough at first, picking one mountain, practising at the edge of your ability, Samuel Johnson's three hours a day, the workshop of obscurity, Confucius and the last basket of earth, and the great soul that Longinus said all great work echoes.

videos.title: The Chess of Life
videos.description:
Life is a kind of chess. Benjamin Franklin wrote that line in an essay on the morals of chess. He believed the game was no idle amusement. It was a training ground for the mind.

Sixty-four squares, thirty-two pieces, rules a child can learn in an afternoon, and more possible games than there are atoms in the observable universe. Your life works the same way. This video plays one game from the first move to the last: the three principles of the opening, the one question strong players ask, why the pawns are the soul of chess, the initiative, sacrifice, the move right after a blunder, and the endgame, where the king you spent the whole game protecting steps forward and fights.

videos.title: How to Speak Articulately
videos.description:
Find your philosophy. Then live it. → https://studio.com/bygone-philosophy

The limits of my language mean the limits of my world. Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote that a century ago, and it may be one of the most quietly devastating sentences in philosophy.

Being articulate is not about big words. It is clear thinking, made audible. In this video we build it from the ground up, with Cato the Elder, Aristotle, Pascal, Zeno and Seneca: know your point, give it a spine, cut the filler, use silence, grow your vocabulary, listen, and think before you speak. It ends with a thirty-day practice you can start today.

videos.title: The Masculine Inner Monologue
videos.description:
"For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he." — Proverbs 23:7

You are not what you say out loud. You are what you repeat to yourself when no one is listening. This video is about that voice: where it really came from, why most of it was never yours, and how a grounded, masculine man learns to take command of it.

You'll learn the grammar of a strong mind, the three voices men use when they fail (and the only one that works), why moods are weather but identity is climate, and how to turn other men from a measuring stick into a map.

videos.title: When Does a Boy Become a Man?
videos.description:
When does a boy become a man? Not when he turns eighteen. The law gives him a vote and a signature. It does not give him a spine.

For most of human history, this question had an answer. There was a day. A rite. A moment the whole community marked: before this, a boy; after this, a man. We have lost that day. In this video, we ask the greats when it actually happens: Rome and the toga of manhood, Homer's Telemachus, Aristotle, Epictetus, King David and Solomon. And at the end, the story of one man who found out.

videos.title: The ENTIRE Philosophy of Schopenhauer in 16:44
videos.description:
Arthur Schopenhauer is remembered as the philosopher of pessimism, but his ideas offer more than gloom: a diagnosis of the human condition, and a surprising kind of cure.

In this video, we walk through his entire philosophy: the world as representation, the blind Will behind everything, why life swings between pain and boredom, and his three paths of escape through art, compassion, and the denial of the will.

We also cover his life and his failed rivalry with Hegel, his views on love, death, free will, and suicide, his influence on Nietzsche, Wagner, and Freud, and the main criticisms of his thought.

videos.title: Nobody Is Coming to Save You
videos.description:
Nobody is coming to save you. It sounds like despair. This video argues it is one of the most freeing sentences in philosophy.

From Kant's "dare to know" to Sartre's condemned freedom, from Viktor Frankl's last freedom to Harriet Tubman's escape and return, we ask why we wait for a rescuer, who we are really waiting for, and what changes when we stop. We also look at why taking responsibility is not the same as blaming yourself for everything that has happened to you.

videos.title: What Makes One a Monster?
videos.description:
What makes a person monstrous? Not a face. Not a birth. In this video, we trace the question across more than two thousand years of philosophy and history, from Aristotle's brutishness and Plato's ring of Gyges, to Hannah Arendt's banality of evil, Stanley Milgram's obedience experiments, the reserve policemen of Józefów, Albert Bandura's moral disengagement, and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein.

And we ask the question that unsettles every easy answer: what if the monster is not the opposite of us, but something we are capable of becoming? And what if every atrocity also depended on the people who could have said no?

videos.title: The Mind of a Workaholic
videos.description:
Napoleon Bonaparte was born on an island France had owned for barely a year. Poor, small, mocked for his accent. By thirty-five, he was Emperor of the French.

So the question isn't whether Napoleon worked hard. The question is what was happening inside that mind, why some people seem to run on a different engine, whether you can build one yourself, and what it costs to run it.

This film takes that mind apart: the hunger that started it, the long hours of preparation behind what looked like genius, the "cabinet of drawers" he used to focus and to rest, the truth about his famous four hours of sleep, his obsession with time and detail, and the cost that ended in Russia and on Saint Helena. Take from it what builds, and leave behind what burns.

videos.title: The Death of the Gravedigger
videos.description:
An old man digs in the snow. he spent his life digging graves. this one is his.

Carlos Schwabe painted a gravedigger at work in a snowy cemetery. He looks up from the pit and finds the Angel of Death waiting above him, a small green light glowing in her hand.

She is not cruel. She is patient. Every grave he ever dug was practice for this one.

videos.title: Win or Die Trying.
videos.description:
Find your philosophy. Then live it. → https://studio.com/bygone-philosophy

Win or die trying.

When a Spartan mother sent her son to war, she handed him his shield and said: with this, or on this. Come home carrying it, or be carried home upon it.

There are only two outcomes. Victory, or death. What's missing is the third option, the one most people live their entire lives inside: running.

This is a film about how to stop quitting, told through 2,500 years of philosophy and art: Caesar crossing the Rubicon, Demosthenes in his underground room, Seneca, Epictetus, Lao Tzu, Aristotle, Nietzsche, Miyamoto Musashi, the Bhagavad Gita, the Hagakure, Socrates, Plato's chariot, Confucius and Diogenes. Why people give up, and how to become the kind of person who doesn't.

"ἢ τὰν ἢ ἐπὶ τᾶς" (with this, or on this). A Spartan mother to her son, as recorded by Plutarch.

videos.title: Fuseli, The Nightmare (1781) #art
videos.description:
In 1781, Henry Fuseli painted a woman asleep with a demon crouched on her chest, while a horse with blank white eyes pushes through the curtains.

Many people see sleep paralysis in it: waking in the dark, unable to move, with a weight on your chest and the feeling that something is in the room.

"Mare" was an old word for a spirit that sat on sleepers' chests. The horse is often read as Fuseli's pun.

The Nightmare — Henry Fuseli, 1781. Detroit Institute of Arts.

videos.title: The Art of Dostoevsky
videos.description:
Nietzsche called him the only psychologist he had anything to learn from. Freud called his last novel the most magnificent ever written. Einstein said he gave him more than any scientist.

Dostoevsky did not find his truths in books. He found them facing a firing squad in 1849, in four years of chains in Siberia, at the roulette tables of Germany, in front of Holbein's Dead Christ in Basel, and at the grave of his three-year-old son. This film follows seven of those truths through his life, his novels and the paintings he loved: Notes from Underground, Crime and Punishment, The Idiot and The Brothers Karamazov.

"Life is a gift, life is happiness; every minute could be an age of happiness." Dostoevsky to his brother Mikhail, 22 December 1849, the evening after his mock execution

videos.title: Are Teens REALLY More Anxious Than Ever?! 😱 #shorts
videos.description:
So are teenagers more anxious than ever before? Here is the honest answer, and it is more complicated than the headlines.

A study in the American Journal of Public Health in 2026 found that among young adults aged 18 to 25, daily anxiety rose from 15% to 19.5% between 2020 and 2024, and the odds of frequent anxiety rose by 28%. But notice the words: young adults, not teenagers.

And now the counter-evidence, because honesty means showing both sides. A huge meta-analysis called Kids These Days, covering 175 studies and more than 400,000 young people between 1981 and 2019, found no rise at all in total emotional and behavioural problems over forty years. Small rises in anxiety reports, yes, but no collapse of a generation — and the data stop before Covid.

So here is the truth. Recent American numbers are up, but the long view says teenagers are not simply broken. What is genuinely new is not the feeling. It is the science. For the first time, we can see anxiety in the brain, at eleven years old, in a circuit we can name.

The Boston Children's Hospital study (Imaging Neuroscience, 1 October 2026, 3,499 young people, median age 12) found the anxiety circuit — amygdala, thalamus and cerebellum — wired differently in teenagers with higher anxiety. This is an association, not a cause: the study does not prove the circuit differences cause anxiety, or the other way round.

Watch the full video: https://youtu.be/BOzWcOcvqQk

#shorts #psychology #franklyexplained #teenanxiety #anxie

videos.title: Why Anxiety Hits Girls 3X Harder?! 😱 #shorts
videos.description:
Why are girls hit harder by anxiety? In the same JAMA Pediatrics study, about 11 in 100 girls had severe anxiety symptoms, compared with about 4 in 100 boys. Nearly three times as many.

The numbers come from a study published in JAMA Pediatrics on 12 October 2026. Researchers led by Bommersbach analysed 15,730 American teenagers aged 12–20 from the 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health, using a standard screening questionnaire called the GAD-7. They found about 11% of girls had severe anxiety symptoms, compared with about 4% of boys.

And it is not just one study. A study published in February 2026 in Frontiers in Psychiatry, comparing more than 8,000 students in China with records from twenty years earlier, found anxiety symptoms had risen in girls across almost every type, with school phobia rising the most.

Why? Scientists think it is a mix of things. Girls, on average, go through puberty earlier, and puberty can make the brain's alarm system more sensitive. Girls also face stronger social pressure, and social media turns all of that into a scoreboard that never switches off. Girls are also more likely to ruminate, replaying a worry again and again instead of letting it go.

Boys are not immune, not even close, and part of the gap may be that boys are less likely to say how they feel. But the pattern is consistent across studies: in the teenage years, anxiety lands harder on girls.

A screening score is not a diagnosis — only a doctor diagnoses.

Watch the full vid

videos.description:
Astronomers have discovered supermassive black holes in the early universe that challenge our current understanding of physics.

These massive objects weigh billions of times the mass of our sun, yet they appeared shortly after the Big Bang. According to standard models of black hole growth, there simply has not been enough time for them to reach such immense sizes through natural accumulation.

Finding these structures so soon after the universe began suggests that our theories regarding cosmic evolution are incomplete. This exploration covers the tension between observation and established astrophysics, detailing why these objects remain an impossible mystery to researchers.

Exploring island geography reveals the complex forces shaping our coastlines and the remote ecosystems that define them.

This discussion examines the geological and physical characteristics of isolated landmasses. Through the lens of island geography, we look at the interplay between rocky shores and oceanic forces to understand how these features evolve over time.

By observing coastal scenery firsthand, we can better appreciate the specific environmental pressures found in these regions. The visual documentation provides a closer look at the terrain and the unique challenges faced by island ecosystems that remain separated from the mainland. Studying these remote landscapes helps clarify the natural history preserved in isolated environments.

videos.title: Why Space Travel is Actually Impossible
videos.description:
Understanding the rocket equation is the first step to mastering the physics of space travel. Learn why current propulsion limits our reach into the galaxy.

This breakdown covers the fundamental limitations of chemical propulsion and the harsh reality of why reaching other stars is so difficult. If you have ever wondered about the math behind heavy launches and why we cannot simply strap more fuel to a rocket, this explanation clarifies the core engineering constraints involved.

We also explore theoretical concepts like warp speed and wormholes to see if they offer a viable path forward. By analyzing the tyranny of the rocket equation, you will gain a clearer picture of the energy requirements needed to traverse the cosmos and why our current methods of space travel remain restricted to our local neighborhood.

videos.title: This Is How Earth Actually Moves Through Space
videos.description: How does the Solar System really move through the Milky Way, and are those viral spiral animations actually correct? In this video, we break down the true motion of Earth and the Sun using reference frames, orbital mechanics, the ecliptic plane, the Solar System barycenter, Milankovitch cycles, the Sun’s galactic orbit, vertical oscillations through the Milky Way, the Oort Cloud, dark matter detection, DAMA/LIBRA, COSINE-100, ANAIS-112, the Great Attractor, and the Cosmic Microwave Background. We explain why Earth does not have one single “true” trajectory, why the planets do not trail behind the Sun like a vortex, how the Solar System moves through our galaxy, and how scientists measure our motion relative to the CMB. This science documentary is for viewers interested in astronomy, astrophysics, space, NASA-style explanations, the Milky Way, dark matter, orbital motion, and the real physics behind popular space myths.

videos.description:
What is actually above the Solar System, and why is flying straight up from the planetary plane harder than reaching Pluto? This space documentary explores orbital mechanics, delta-v, gravity assists, the ecliptic plane, the heliosphere, heliopause, Oort Cloud, Scholz’s Star, Local Interstellar Cloud, Local Bubble, ancient supernova explosions, iron-60 on Earth, the Sagittarius Stream, Fermi Bubbles, the Milky Way’s dark matter halo, and the true structure of our cosmic neighborhood. We also examine NASA and ESA missions including Voyager 2, Ulysses, and Solar Orbiter, explain why humanity still has no real top-down photograph of the entire Solar System, and reveal why there is no universal “up” in space. This video is for viewers interested in astronomy, astrophysics, space exploration, NASA missions, the Milky Way, the Solar System, and scientifically accurate explanations of how the Universe really works.

videos.title: Why Humanity is Stuck at Type 0 (And May Never Reach Type I)
videos.description: How advanced is humanity on the Kardashev Scale, and what would it take to become a Type I, Type II, or Type III civilization? In this video, we explore humanity’s current Type 0 status, global energy consumption, fusion power, planetary engineering, Dyson Swarms, Tabby’s Star, alien megastructures, infrared waste heat, Project G-HAT, SETI, the Fermi Paradox, and the Great Filter. We also examine Nikolai Kardashev’s original 1964 scale, Carl Sagan’s continuous version, John Barrow’s scale of miniaturization, and the search for advanced extraterrestrial civilizations across the Milky Way. Could humanity harness the energy of an entire planet, star, or galaxy, or will technological risks, nuclear weapons, engineered pathogens, climate change, and artificial intelligence prevent us from reaching the next stage of civilization?

videos.title: Voyager 1 Is 15 Billion Miles Away. Here’s What It Found
videos.description: How are Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 still communicating with Earth after nearly 50 years and more than 24 billion kilometers of travel? This video explores the Voyager mission, the Grand Tour and gravity assists, NASA’s Deep Space Network, discoveries beyond the heliosphere, the probes’ fading nuclear power, and the Golden Records they will carry through interstellar space long after contact is lost. A cinematic deep dive for anyone fascinated by space exploration, astronomy, and humanity’s farthest spacecraft.

In this video, we explore the biggest mysteries at the edge of modern cosmology: ancient James Webb galaxies that formed too fast, colossal structures like the Big Ring and Giant Arc, new DESI data suggesting dark energy may be changing over time, and the terrifying problem of the singularity. From the Cosmic Microwave Background and dark matter to eternal inflation, the holographic principle, the Big Bounce, and Roger Penrose’s Conformal Cyclic Cosmology, this is a journey into what may have existed before the Big Bang - and why the beginning of time might be stranger than we ever imagined.

videos.title: Something’s Wrong With Our Galaxy’s Black Hole
videos.description:
Hear the sonified NASA X-ray data from Sagittarius A star, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. Learn how an ancient galactic flare nearly stripped Earth's ozone layer.

This video explains how researchers convert raw astronomy data into audio to study the violent history of our galaxy. By analyzing this sonified NASA X-ray data, we can trace the path of energy emissions that originated from the very heart of the Milky Way center. It is a direct look at the powerful forces shaping our cosmic neighborhood.

We break down the specific gravitational event involving Sagittarius A star and what its activity means for planetary habitability. Understanding how this supermassive black hole functions helps us contextualize the radiation risks present in our galaxy. This examination is designed for space enthusiasts interested in the intersection of astrophysics and data representation.

Subscribe for weekly space science breakdowns, and let me know in the comments if you want to hear more sonified data from deep space.

What would happen if a human body was dragged through the 0th, 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th dimensions?
