videos.title: Why Earth Stopped Building Monsters ?
videos.description:
For most of Earth's history, being enormous was the winning strategy. The air was so rich in oxygen that dragonflies grew the wingspan of a bird of prey and centipedes reached the length of a grown man. Then the vertebrates took the idea further.

On land, herbivores hollowed their own vertebrae into air-filled chambers so their skeletons could carry the weight, and cracked their tails through the air at supersonic speed. The hunters answered with serrated teeth the size of railroad spikes and bites measured in thousands of pounds per square inch.

The oceans went further, because water carries what bone cannot. Long-necked hunters looked like a serpent threaded through the body of a giant turtle. Overhead flew animals as tall as a giraffe, with skulls over nine feet long, launching into the air off all four limbs.

Bone fused into helmets over the skull, tails ended in clubs that could snap a predator's leg, and horned herds locked into circles with the young inside. Then the volcanoes opened, the climate began to swing, and being enormous became the thing that killed them.

So what does it take to build a monster - and why did Earth stop making them?

Settle in for the full story, and subscribe for more documentaries on Earth's deep past.

videos.title: Heat Death, Big Rip or Big Crunch: How Does It All End? | Full Documentary
videos.description:
Everything that exists is running down. Stars burn through their fuel, galaxies drift apart, entropy only ever increases - so the universe has an ending, and physics has narrowed it to a short list of candidates. The leading one is the big freeze: expansion continues forever, star formation stops, and the cosmos cools toward a temperature just above absolute zero.

The alternatives are stranger. If dark energy strengthens with time, the big rip tears apart galaxies, then stars, then planets, then atoms themselves in a final accelerating instant. If it reverses, everything collapses back into a big crunch. And if our vacuum is only metastable, a bubble of true vacuum could appear anywhere, expand at the speed of light, and rewrite physics with no warning at all.

The likeliest ending is the slowest. Protons may decay. Black holes inherit an empty cosmos, then evaporate through Hawking radiation, the largest taking longer than any number worth writing down.

So how does everything actually end - and does time still mean anything afterwards?

Settle in for the full story, and subscribe for more feature-length documentaries on space and deep time.

videos.title: The Future of the Universe: Everything That Happens After Us | Full Documentary
videos.description:
The universe is 13.8 billion years old, and it is barely getting started. In about a billion years the Sun will be bright enough to boil the oceans away. In roughly four and a half billion, the Milky Way will collide with Andromeda and the night sky will be rebuilt. And in five billion, the Sun will swell into a red giant, swallow the inner planets, and then collapse into a white dwarf no bigger than Earth.

That is only the first chapter. Star formation will slow and then stop. The last red dwarfs will burn for trillions of years before the final one goes dark, and accelerating expansion will carry every other galaxy beyond the horizon, until the sky visible from here is empty - a universe where no future astronomer could ever discover that other galaxies exist.

Then even matter runs out of time. If protons decay, ordinary material simply dissolves. Black holes inherit what is left, feeding in the dark for spans there are no useful names for, until Hawking radiation bleeds away even the largest of them. What remains is heat death: maximum entropy, no gradients, nothing left that can happen.

So does everything end cold and quiet - or does it tear itself apart first?

Settle in for the full story, and subscribe for more feature-length documentaries on space and deep time.

videos.title: A 9-Foot Skull That Bit an Ichthyosaur Clean in Half
videos.description:
For five hundred million years Earth has been running one experiment: which weapon wins? The answer keeps changing. In the Cambrian seas it was Anomalocaris, the first hunter with real eyes. In the Ordovician it was Cameroceras, a twenty-foot cone of stone drifting through the dark like a missile.
 
Then the arms race escalated. Dunkleosteus turned its skull into a pair of bone shears. Otodus megalodon abandoned armour for sheer scale and closed its seven-foot jaws with up to forty thousand pounds of force. In the Carboniferous, oxygen reached thirty-five percent and the arthropods grew into it: Arthropleura at eight and a half feet, and Meganeura, a dragonfly the size of an eagle, hunting a sky with nothing else in it.
 
On land came Tyrannosaurus rex, Spinosaurus and the sickle-clawed Utahraptor. Offshore, in the seas nicknamed Hell's Aquarium, Mosasaurus swallowed prey whole while Pliosaurus funkei drove a nine-foot skull through an ichthyosaur and split it in half. After the asteroid, Smilodon populator and the short-faced bear Arctodus simus took the empty throne.
 
But the deadliest animal on this planet never needed size at all. It weighs two and a half milligrams, has no teeth and no claws, and it kills hundreds of thousands of people every year.
 
So what really makes a creature deadly - force, or reach?
 
Settle in for the full story, and subscribe for more feature-length documentaries on Earth's deep past.
 
#DeadliestCreatures #PrehistoricEarth #Documentary

videos.title: Earth's Most Violent Catastrophe Wasn't an Asteroid
videos.description:
There were no polar ice caps. Forests reached into high latitudes, reefs crowded the warm shallow seas, and the climate had been stable for millions of years. Nothing in that world suggested what was coming. Then the crust split open along thousands of fissures, and up to 90 to 96 percent of all marine species were wiped out, along with roughly 70 percent of land vertebrates.
 
This is the most violent event in the planet's history, and it did not arrive in a single afternoon. Flood basalts poured out for longer than our species has existed. Sulfur aerosols dimmed the sun and chilled the surface; when they washed out, the carbon dioxide left behind drove temperatures hard the other way. The oceans warmed, lost their oxygen and turned acidic, and bacteria in the stagnant depths filled the water with hydrogen sulfide.
 
Then came the long night. Phytoplankton collapsed and took the marine food web down with them. Reefs disappeared. Forests burned and their soils washed into the sea. Trilobites, which had survived everything for hundreds of millions of years, were gone for good, and ferns and mosses inherited the emptied ground.
 
All of it is still readable in the rock: carbon isotope excursions in limestone, black shales laid down in oxygen-free water, mercury spikes from volcanic ash, spore layers where forests failed, and ancient temperatures locked inside fossil shells.

videos.title: Why Everything on Earth Almost Died 252 Million Years Ago | Documentary
videos.description:
Two hundred and sixty million years ago, Earth was thriving. The continents were fused into Pangaea, vast glossopteris forests covered the southern hemisphere, gorgonopsians hunted with saber-like teeth, and reefs crowded the shallow seas. Then, in a geological instant, nearly 90% of all marine species and around 70% of land vertebrates were gone. The end-Permian extinction - the Great Dying - is the closest life has ever come to being erased.

The killer was Siberia. For roughly a million years, fissures in the crust poured out between one and four million cubic kilometres of lava. What survives of it still covers two million square kilometres, an area larger than Mexico. As magma forced its way upward it burned through buried coal, venting carbon dioxide, methane, sulfur dioxide and halogen gases straight into the atmosphere. For scale: when Mount Tambora erupted in 1815, it chilled the planet enough that 1816 became known as the Year Without a Summer. Siberia did that for a million years.

Global temperatures climbed by ten to fifteen degrees Celsius - roughly twice the difference between the last ice age and today. Warming oceans lost their oxygen, and bacteria in the anoxic depths filled the water with hydrogen sulfide. Acid rain stripped the forests. The ozone layer thinned. Around the equator, the fossil record simply goes blank.

videos.title: Before Fire, the Night Belonged to the Predators | Full Documentary
videos.description:
Two million years ago, our ancestors were not the confident hunters we like to imagine. They were small, lightly built primates with no claws, no fangs and no speed, sharing the African savanna with animals that regarded them as food. And the bones tell the story: some fossilized hominin remains carry puncture wounds and gnaw marks matching the teeth of large carnivores.

This full documentary is the story of the predators that hunted us, and how a defenceless primate outlasted every one of them. It begins with the saber toothed cats. Smilodon, whose canines reached seven inches and curved like daggers, killed by grappling prey down and driving those teeth into the throat. In Eurasia and Africa, the taller, slender Homotherium held its own territory. The La Brea Tar Pits have yielded thousands of Smilodon skeletons.

Then came the hunters that worked together. The dire wolf, Canis dirus, was heavier than any wolf alive today, with a bite strong enough to crack bone, and hunted in coordinated packs that exploited exactly what humans could not hide - an injured adult, a slow elder, a child at the edge of the group. Alongside it, the giant short faced hyena Pachycrocuta brevirostris outweighed any hyena alive now.

Others overwhelmed by size alone. Arctodus simus, the short faced bear, stood over five feet at the shoulder and eleven feet when it reared - solitary, unpredictable, and impossible to negotiate with over a carcass. And the danger was not only mammalian: terror birds

videos.title: The 4 Billion Years of Earth History Nobody Ever Taught You | Full Documentary
videos.description:
For more than four and a half billion years, Earth existed without a single human being on it. Continents collided, mountains rose and eroded to dust, and whole dynasties of life ruled the planet and vanished before our species took its first step. If Earth's history were compressed into a single day, humans would appear in the final seconds before midnight. Everything before that is the forgotten age.

This full documentary walks that timeline from the beginning - a molten world under constant bombardment, then chemistry crossing into biology in the hydrothermal dark around 3.8 billion years ago. For two billion years, life stays microscopic. Then cyanobacteria begin releasing oxygen, a waste gas so reactive it poisoned much of the living world and rusted the iron out of the seas, and the Great Oxidation Event makes complex life possible.

From there it accelerates. Soft-bodied Ediacaran organisms drift across the seafloor 600 million years ago. The Cambrian explosion arms the oceans with shells, eyes and jaws. Plants green the continents 470 million years ago, animals follow them ashore, and the age of reptiles begins on Pangaea. Sauropods over 80 feet long move through Jurassic forests while pterosaurs with 30-foot wingspans cross the coast above them.

videos.title: The First Monster to Walk on Land | Full Documentary
videos.description:
For four billion years, nothing walked. The continents were bare rock and drifting sand, without a single footprint anywhere on Earth. Then something dragged itself out of the water — and the planet was never the same.

The story begins more than 400 million years ago, in the Devonian, in warm shallow swamps and shrinking river pools. Among the fish there was a group called the lobe-finned fish, whose fins were built around bones arranged like a limb: one bone, then two, then a spray of smaller ones. In 2004, on Ellesmere Island in the Canadian Arctic, paleontologists found the most famous of them. Tiktaalik roseae, 375 million years old, had scales and gills like a fish, but also a flat crocodile-like skull, a neck it could turn, sturdy shoulders, and spiracles on top of its head for gulping air.

Tiktaalik never strode across dry ground; it propped itself up in the shallows. But close behind came Acanthostega, with fully formed digits — eight on each hand, not five — on limbs still too weak to carry its weight. Then Ichthyostega, reinforced vertebrae and stronger limbs, hauling itself forward. Then Tulerpeton, six digits per limb, venturing further from water than anything before it.

The land they entered was brutal. Gravity crushed bodies that water had always held up. Gills collapsed in open air. Permeable skin bled moisture away. They breathed by buccal pumping, forcing air down by lowering the floor of the mouth, because ribs had not yet learned the job.

videos.title: The Day Oceans Became Graveyards | Documentary
videos.description:
Seventy-one percent of this planet is water, and more than eighty percent of all life on Earth lives inside it. For most of human history the ocean seemed infinite — too vast to empty, too deep to poison. Within a single lifetime, we proved that wrong. This is the story of how the richest ecosystems on Earth became graveyards, and of the warnings we chose not to hear.

After the Second World War, industrial fishing fleets grew larger and faster than anything the ocean had ever faced. In the North Atlantic, cod had fed coastal economies for centuries — and by the early 1990s, a stock that once seemed inexhaustible collapsed. Scientists had recommended catch limits years earlier. They were softened, delayed, ignored.

Then came the plastic. The Great Pacific Garbage Patch spans an area larger than Texas and holds an estimated eighty thousand metric tons of debris — and floating debris is the smaller half of the problem. Microplastics have been found in deep sea sediments thousands of meters down, in fish sold at market, and in animals no human has ever seen alive.

Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor yet support roughly twenty-five percent of all marine species, and they are bleaching faster than they can recover. The Great Barrier Reef suffered mass bleaching in 2016, 2017, and again in the years that followed. videos.title: When Earth Was Hell | Full Documentary
videos.description:
For most of its history, Earth was actively hostile to anything trying to live on it. Its first eon is named after the Greek underworld: the Hadean. There were oceans of magma, no oxygen to breathe, no ozone layer to stop incoming ultraviolet radiation, acid rain falling into acidic seas, and days that ended in less than ten hours.

Then the sky began raining fire. Between roughly 4.1 and 3.8 billion years ago, during the Late Heavy Bombardment, shifting orbits in the outer solar system flung debris toward the inner planets. Impacts large enough to vaporize entire oceans struck again and again, sterilizing the surface and melting the crust back into liquid rock. The cratered face of the Moon is still a record of it.

This full documentary travels through every one of Earth's deadliest chapters. Archean volcanism that filled the air with sulfur and turned rain to acid. Snowball Earth, when ice may have reached the equator between 720 and 635 million years ago and sealed the oceans beneath it. The Great Oxygen Catastrophe of 2.4 billion years ago, when cyanobacteria flooded the atmosphere with a gas that was lethal poison to almost everything then alive, causing what may have been the first mass extinction, driven by life itself.

And then the Great Dying. Around 252 million years ago the Siberian Traps erupted for hundreds of thousands of years, acidifying the oceans and stripping them of oxygen until 90 percent of marine species and 70 percent of land vertebrates were gone. E

For more than 160 million years, dinosaurs had dominated the planet. Tyrannosaurus rex hunted across ancient floodplains, Triceratops moved in herds, giant pterosaurs ruled the skies, and mosasaurs controlled the oceans. Then, in a matter of seconds, their world began to collapse.

videos.title: Every Dinosaur Dynasty, From The First To The Last
videos.description:
The dinosaurs did not conquer the Earth. They inherited it — twice — from catastrophes that nearly ended life itself.

This documentary tells the whole story, from the ruined world that came before them to the single day it all ended, and what survived afterward.

It opens 252 million years ago, at the end of the Permian, with the worst event in the history of life. The Great Dying erased roughly ninety percent of marine species and seventy percent of land vertebrates. Siberian volcanoes burned for hundreds of thousands of years. Oceans lost their oxygen. Acid rain fell across continents. What crawled out of that wreckage was not a dinosaur — it was a modest group of reptiles called archosaurs, and for tens of millions of years the dinosaurs among them were nobody. The apex predators of the Triassic were crocodile relatives, six-metre rauisuchians that ruled the river valleys while the first dinosaurs lived in their shadow.

Those first dinosaurs were unimpressive. Eoraptor — the name means dawn thief — was about a metre long and probably ate insects. Then, 201 million years ago, a second mass extinction wiped out the competition. The crocodile-line rulers vanished. The dinosaurs didn't.

Everything after that is escalation.

The Jurassic turned them into giants: Brachiosaurus, Diplodocus and Apatosaurus past twenty-five metres and forty tons, held up by hollow air-filled bones and bird-like lungs, with necks longer than a city bus. Allosaurus rose to hunt them with a hatchet

videos.title: This Shrimp Creates Temperatures Hotter Than The Sun's Surface
videos.description:
In 1799, a dried animal skin arrived in London and a respected zoologist named George Shaw took a pair of scissors to it — hunting for the taxidermy stitches he was certain a fraudster had used to sew a duck's bill onto a mammal. There were no stitches. The platypus was real. And it would take another eighty-five years, and a telegram from a researcher in Australia in 1884, before science accepted the rest of it: that this mammal lays eggs.

That reaction — flat disbelief, followed by evidence that refuses to go away — is the thread running through this entire documentary.

We look at the okapi, known to people living alongside it for centuries and dismissed by Western naturalists as a confused mash-up of donkey, zebra and giraffe until skin samples reached the Natural History Museum in 1901. The giant squid, filed under sailors' folklore and Norse kraken myths until bodies started washing up in Newfoundland in the 1870s — thirteen meters long, with eyes the size of dinner plates, and still not photographed alive until 2004. And the coelacanth, a lobe-finned fish believed to have died with the dinosaurs 66 million years ago, until a South African museum curator named Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer took a phone call from a fisherman in December 1938. The ichthyologist she sent her sketch to said it was like watching a ghost walk into his laboratory.

videos.title: The World After Humans Disappear
videos.description:
No war. No asteroid. No plague. Every human being on Earth simply vanishes in a single instant — and everything we ever built is left standing exactly where we abandoned it, still running, with no one left to hold it together.

This is what happens next.

Within the first hour, power plants begin tripping their automatic shutdowns with no operators to correct them. Within 48 hours, most of the planet is dark, and the artificial glow visible from space for over a century simply blinks out. Planes still in the air run out of fuel and come down. Fires start in restaurant kitchens and empty living rooms with no one to call for help, and burn until they run out of things to consume. Beneath New York, the pumps that hold back the groundwater stop, and the subway system begins filling with dark water within days.

Then the slow part begins — and it belongs entirely to nature.

Rain finds every clogged gutter and unsealed crack. Freeze and thaw widens them, winter after winter. Seeds land in broken asphalt, and within a decade a parking lot becomes a meadow. Steel rebar rusts inside concrete and splits skyscrapers open from within. Glass falls from towers and turns office floors into forest floor. Bridges that were never meant to go a single year without inspection — the Golden Gate, the Brooklyn Bridge, Tower Bridge — lose their fight against rust and wind one by one. Dams fail, and rivers that were controlled for generations run wild again.

videos.title: The Ocean Was Once Worse Than Space | Full Documentary
videos.description:
For centuries we looked up. We dreamed of rockets, of the Moon, of the stars — while the single most hostile, least understood environment on Earth sat directly beneath our feet, unseen and untouched. In the early twentieth century, scientists knew more about the surface of the Moon than they did about the bottom of the sea. Light cannot reach it. Radio cannot penetrate it. And the pressure at its deepest point exceeds fifteen thousand pounds on every square inch — enough to destroy a vessel faster than the human nervous system can register that anything has gone wrong.

This is the story of the frontier humanity almost ignored, and the people who refused to.

It begins in 1930 off the coast of Bermuda, where a naturalist named William Beebe and an engineer named Otis Barton climbed into a four-and-a-half-foot steel ball called the Bathysphere, allowed the hatch to be bolted shut from the outside, and were lowered into total darkness on a single cable — with no engine, no steering, and no possibility of rescue. It runs through the Cold War depth race, where the Trieste carried Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh nearly eleven thousand meters down into the Challenger Deep in January 1960, listening to the hull crack at nine thousand meters and deciding to continue anyway. videos.title: What Lived Before the First Dinosaur? | Full Documentary
videos.description:
The first dinosaur did not appear until about 230 million years ago. For more than a hundred million years before that, Earth already had rulers — apex predators, giant herbivores, food webs that rose and collapsed — and almost none of them have names you would know. This is the world dinosaurs inherited.

It begins in the Carboniferous, 359 to 299 million years ago. Oxygen made up as much as 35 percent of the atmosphere against 21 percent today, and insects grew to match: dragonflies with two-foot wingspans patrolled the air. Below them amphibians ruled — Eryops in the shallows, Diplocaulus with its boomerang-shaped skull. Then, around 315 million years ago, a small lizard-like creature called Hylonomus did something no vertebrate had done: it laid an egg that did not need water.

That innovation opened the planet's dry interior. As Pangaea assembled and the swamps retreated, reptiles spread inland and split into two lineages: one led to lizards, crocodiles and dinosaurs, the other to the synapsids — Dimetrodon, the sail-backed hunter almost everyone mistakes for a dinosaur, and later the therapsids, from beaked dicynodonts to Inostrancevia, a gorgonopsian with saber-like canines projecting from its upper jaw. Among the small cynodonts, our own lineage was quietly taking shape.

videos.title: Before T. rex, Something Worse Ruled the Earth | Full Documentary
videos.description:
Long before the roar of Tyrannosaurus rex echoed across the Late Cretaceous floodplains, another predator ruled Earth with an efficiency few creatures in the planet's history have ever matched. It left behind no blockbuster fame and no household name. Yet in its time it was death incarnate — a hunter so perfectly adapted that entire ecosystems arranged themselves around its presence.

To find it we travel back hundreds of millions of years, to a world of supercontinents, giant ferns and towering horsetails, where armored fish and early sharks patrolled shallow reefs. In that arena this predator emerged — and then simply stopped changing. Generation after generation its core design held, and when natural selection stops adjusting, it usually means a creature has reached near perfection for its niche.

Its power was engineered from the skull down: reinforced bone built to absorb enormous stress, teeth that were weapons in their own right, forward-facing eyes for depth perception, a neck of pure muscle to drive the head like a hammer. But anatomy is only potential. What made it lethal was patience — waiting motionless at a water's edge or a natural choke point, then releasing everything at once.

So why has almost no one heard of it? Partly timing — it lived before the dinosaurs the world learned to love. Partly habitat, because waterlogged environments fossilize poorly. And partly appearance: no horns, no sail, no towering silhouette, just a streamlined and brutally functional

videos.title: The Largest Animals Earth Has Ever Seen | Full Documentary
videos.description:
The largest animal in the history of life on Earth is not a dinosaur, and it is not extinct. It is swimming in the ocean right now. A blue whale reaches thirty meters and two hundred tons, with a heart that weighs as much as a small car and a tongue as heavy as an elephant, and it survives entirely on krill, some of the smallest animals in the sea.

On land, gravity sets harder limits, and the record belongs to the sauropods. Argentinosaurus stretched beyond thirty meters and may have weighed a hundred tons, its femur alone more than two meters long. Patagotitan rivaled it. Giraffatitan browsed twelve meters above the ground. They managed it with bones filled with air sacs, pillar like legs, and necks over fifteen meters long that let them strip vegetation without moving. By comparison, Tyrannosaurus rex weighed nine tons, formidable but a fraction of the herbivores it lived alongside.

The ancient oceans produced their own monsters. Shonisaurus, an ichthyosaur over twenty meters long. Kronosaurus, with a skull nearly three meters across. Mosasaurus, seventeen meters of double hinged jaws. Leedsichthys, a twenty meter fish that filtered plankton long before whales did. And Megalodon, an eighteen meter shark with serrated teeth the size of a human hand and one of the strongest bites ever measured in a vertebrate.

Then came the giants of ice and air. Woolly mammoths weighing ten tons, carrying tusks over four meters long. Megatherium, a ground sloth six meters tall. Paracerath

videos.title: Prehistoric Earth: The Lost World Hidden Beneath Antarctica | Full Documentary Movie
videos.description:
From above, Antarctica looks like nothing at all. A blank sheet of white where winter temperatures fall below minus eighty degrees Celsius and no rock breaks the surface for hundreds of kilometers in any direction. For most of human history, that blankness was the whole story. Then instruments began listening through the ice, and the continent turned out to be hiding an entire world.

Seismic surveys and ice penetrating radar found mountains where there should have been flat bedrock. The Gamburtsev Subglacial Mountains rise as high as the European Alps, yet not one summit breaks through the surface. Radar also revealed valleys, rift systems, volcanoes, and basins lying below sea level, a landscape as varied as any exposed continent, sealed under as much as four kilometers of ice.

Then came the water. More than four hundred subglacial lakes have now been identified beneath Antarctica, held liquid by immense pressure and heat rising from the Earth's interior. Lake Vostok, the largest, lies beneath nearly four kilometers of ice and rivals Lake Ontario in size. In 2013, a team drilled into Lake Whillans through eight hundred meters of ice and found thousands of species of microbes living in permanent darkness, feeding on chemistry from rock instead of sunlight.

Antarctica was not always frozen. Fossil forests and the remains of plant eating dinosaurs describe a temperate, green continent. That world ended around thirty four million years ago, when the Drake Passage opened and c

videos.title: The Day Noon Looked Like Midnight | Full Documentary Movie
videos.description:
It began as an ordinary morning.

The sun was shining. People were heading to work. Children were arriving at school. Farmers were working beneath a clear sky.

Then the light began to disappear.

Before noon, the sky was turning gray. Hours later, the sun was completely gone. Streetlights switched on in the middle of the day. Ash began falling from the sky, temperatures dropped, and an entire valley found itself trapped beneath what looked like an unnatural night.

Beyond the hills, a massive wildfire was generating an enormous column of smoke. The fire became powerful enough to create its own atmospheric system, forming a pyrocumulonimbus cloud capable of carrying smoke tens of thousands of feet upward and spreading it across huge distances.

Day became night.

The next morning came—but daylight didn't.

As smoke and ash continued to block the sun, residents faced hazardous air, evacuations, disrupted wildlife, failing visibility, and the growing possibility that the fire could cross the hills and reach their homes.

This full documentary follows the darkness from its first almost-unnoticeable signs through the wildfire emergency, the science behind the black sky, the struggle to contain the inferno, and the eventual return of sunlight.

It is a story about wildfire, atmospheric science, survival, climate, and what happens when one of the most dependable things in human life—daylight—suddenly disappears.

videos.title: Life Survived 5 Apocalypses: Are We the Sixth? | Full Documentary Movie
videos.description:
Life on Earth has survived disasters almost impossible to imagine.

videos.description:
Democrats have won control of both the U.S. House and Senate following the 2026 midterm elections. What does the shift in power mean for federal workers, DOGE job cuts and the future of the federal workforce under President Donald Trump?

On this episode of **Federal Workforce Fallout**, WUSA9's Larry Miller examines what a Democratic-controlled Congress could mean for thousands of federal employees and contractors who lost their jobs during the Trump administration's efforts to shrink the federal government.

**In this episode:**

- **DOGE investigations:** Democrats are promising new congressional oversight of Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), federal layoffs and government spending.
- **2026 midterm election results:** Political correspondent Scott MacFarlane breaks down the Democratic victories, the changing balance of power in Washington and what Congress can realistically accomplish with President Trump still in the White House.
- **Federal jobs in Virginia:** Reps. James Walkinshaw and Suhas Subramanyam discuss protecting federal workers, restoring government programs and addressing the rising cost of living in Northern Virginia.
- **Former federal workers elected to Congress:** Meet former government employees who won House seats after campaigning against federal workforce cuts.

videos.title: How the Biggest House on Millionaire's Row Connects to the American Revolution | Undiscovered DC
videos.description:
Matt Gregory and Carolyn Muraskin of DC Design Tours explore how this historic mansion became the headquarters for the Society of the Cincinnati, the oldest fraternal organization in the United States.

After Larz Anderson died, Isabel Adnderson donated the estate to the organization, whose first president was George Washington and second president was Alexander Hamilton. To be a member to this day, you must be able to trace your lineage back to a commissioned officer who fought in the American Revolution.

Along the way, Matt shares a bit of "Matt history" regarding the Sons of the American Revolution, and confesses that the Gregorys were actually Loyalists!

Want to see the full tour of D.C.'s historic mansions? Watch the full episode now in our playlist!

videos.title: TEXAS 1974 Cold Case SOLVED — She Went to Celebrate Valentine's Night With Her Boyfriend...
videos.description:
In February 1974, Carla Walker was seventeen years old, a high school student from Fort Worth, Texas, with her whole life ahead of her. On the night of February 16th, she went out with her boyfriend, Rodney McCoy, to celebrate Valentine’s Day weekend. They stopped at Ridglea Bowl, expecting an ordinary end to their evening.

Then, in the bowling alley parking lot, a stranger attacked Rodney and took Carla.

Three days later, investigators searching near Benbrook Lake made a devastating discovery. Carla’s body had been found inside a drainage culvert, bringing a desperate search to an end and turning the disappearance of a teenage girl into a murder investigation.

Police had a crime scene. They had a surviving witness who had been attacked. And they had a crucial lead connected to the weapon used that night: a magazine associated with a .22 Ruger pistol.

This is the full story — from Carla’s final night and the discovery of her body near Benbrook Lake, through decades of unanswered questions and an investigation that struggled to find the proof it needed, to the man police questioned early on who would eventually be convicted of her murder.

But in 1993, that DNA could not tell investigators who the killer was.

videos.title: Texas 1981 Cold Case — After 45 Years, DNA Led Investigators to Her Killer
videos.description:
In April 1981, Yolanda Herrera was twenty-three years old, living in Universal City, Texas, and trying to build a life after her divorce. On the morning of April 11, Yolanda left Johnny’s Inn and began walking home.

She never made it.

Two days later, two children walking to school discovered Yolanda’s body in a field near East Aviation Drive. Investigators quickly determined that she had been murdered, and evidence recovered from the crime scene would eventually become critical to the case.

There was DNA.


This is the full story — from the night Yolanda Herrera was last seen alive, through decades of unanswered questions and advances in forensic science, to the discarded beer can in Arizona that helped investigators identify the man they believe was responsible for her death.

videos.title: Wisconsin 1974 Cold Case Solved After 50 Years — Her Killer Was Finally Caught at 84
videos.description:
In February 1974, Mary Schlais was twenty-five years old, an accomplished artist and University of Minnesota graduate who had traveled internationally, spoke fluent German, and was learning Japanese. She was heading from Minneapolis toward Chicago for an art show, traveling the way many young people did at the time: hitchhiking across Wisconsin.

Then, along the road, Mary accepted a ride from a stranger.

Investigators would later learn that the man behind the wheel asked her for sexual contact. When she refused, he attacked her with a knife. A witness driving through rural Dunn County saw a man throw a woman's body from a vehicle, and investigators soon discovered Mary along a dead-end road in Spring Brook Township, Wisconsin.

Police had a witness description. They had missing personal belongings. And near the scene, they recovered something that would eventually become one of the most important pieces of evidence in the entire investigation: a stocking hat.

But in 1974, the hat could not tell investigators who had worn it.


This is the full story — from Mary's journey toward Chicago and the brutal attack that ended her life, through fifty years of unanswered questions, false leads, and changing technology, to the piece of evidence that waited half a century for science to finally reveal its owner.

On December 6, 1991, four teenage girls were murdered inside an Austin, Texas yogurt shop. Jennifer Harbison, 17, and her coworker Eliza Thomas, 17, were closing up I Can't Believe It's Yogurt! when Jennifer's younger sister Sarah, 15, and her friend Amy Ayers, 13, arrived to catch a ride home. All four were bound, gagged, and shot. Before leaving, whoever did it set the building on fire.

Investigators recovered a spent shell casing from a floor drain and DNA evidence from the scene — but in 1991, neither could be searched against a national database. A false lead pointed toward four local teenagers. The case went cold for another decade. That match led investigators to a genetic identification already made seven years earlier, in a different state, in a case no one had ever thought to connect to Austin. A final DNA test, run on evidence recovered from one victim's fingernails, confirmed it.

videos.description:
In July 1989, Fawn Marie Cox was sixteen years old, living with her family in Kansas City's Historic Northeast neighborhood and working a summer job at Worlds of Fun, the local amusement park. She'd finished a closing shift, come home, and gone straight to bed — she had another shift the next morning.

Then someone climbed to her second-floor bedroom window, broke through it, and killed her while the rest of her family slept one floor below, the sound covered by window air conditioners running against the summer heat.

Police recovered DNA from the scene. In 1989, that evidence could only be compared against a suspect already in custody — it couldn't be searched. Investigators charged teenage suspects based on a witness statement; the witness later recanted, and the charges were dropped. In the early 2000s, KCPD's crime lab uploaded a DNA profile from the case to CODIS, the national criminal database. No match — the person responsible had never been convicted of an offense requiring a DNA sample, so his profile simply wasn't in the system. The case went cold again.

Then, in the summer of 2020, Operation LeGend brought federal funding into the Kansas City Police Department, and with FBI assistance, detectives ran the crime-scene DNA through forensic genetic genealogy for the first time — the same category of technique that had identified California's Golden State Killer two years earlier. videos.title: WASHINGTON 1986 Cold Case Solved After 32 Years — A Restaurant Napkin Caught Her Killer
videos.description:
WASHINGTON 1986 Cold Case Solved After 32 Years — A Restaurant Napkin Caught Her Killer
-----
In March 1986, 12-year-old Michella Welch rode her bike to Puget Park in Tacoma, Washington, with her two younger sisters. She never came home. Thirty-two years later, a napkin left behind at a restaurant table gave detectives the lead they had waited decades for.
This documentary follows the case through the long years it stayed cold. It covers the search on that March day, the original investigation, and a second Tacoma girl, Jennifer Bastian, who was lost just months later. It also covers the 2016 discovery that two different men were responsible. Then we follow the detectives and genetic genealogists who would not let the case go, and the breakthrough that changed everything.
Michella was a big sister, a bike rider, and a daughter who is still deeply missed. This video is made with respect for her, her family, and everyone in Tacoma who waited for answers.

For fifty years, the Dunn County Sheriff's Office and the Wisconsin Division of Criminal Investigation followed tips, interviewed witnesses and re-examined the evidence as science advanced. An eyewitness had seen a man and a vehicle, but no viable suspect emerged.

A knit cap left at the scene held the best chance. Hairs on it produced no match in the national DNA database, so in 2023 the sheriff's office turned to investigative genetic genealogy with the Ramapo College team led by Professor David Gurney.

Two relatives were examined and ruled out before an adoption changed the search. In the fall of 2024, another relative's DNA pointed to a name no family tree had shown. On what would have been Mary's 76th birthday, the match was confirmed.

In March 2025, the case ended in a Wisconsin courtroom with a no-contest plea and a sentence of life in prison.

In April 1981, a young woman was found beside Greenlee Road near Troy, Ohio, wearing a handmade fringed buckskin jacket. She carried no identification. The most startling detail was that nobody had ever reported her missing.

This documentary follows the case through nearly four decades as a cold case. It covers the fingerprints, dental records and composite drawings that led nowhere. It covers the town that laid her to rest as a stranger and the scientific clues hidden in her clothing. Then it turns to the 2018 breakthrough, when volunteers used genetic genealogy to turn a preserved sample into a name, and to the family who never stopped searching.

Her name was Marcia Lenore Sossoman King. She was 21, from Little Rock, Arkansas, and we remember her here as a daughter, a sister and a mother, not only as a case file.

On Sunday, September 15, 1963, fourteen-year-old Addie Mae Collins was getting ready to sing on Youth Day at Sixteenth Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, Alabama. A warning call came just minutes before a blast at the east steps. Four girls lost their lives.

Within two years the FBI had names, informant recordings and a list of men it held responsible. But the federal case was closed in 1968 and the files were sealed. A state trial in 1977 convicted only one man.

In 1995 the FBI reopened the case and unsealed thousands of pieces of evidence. Old reel-to-reel tapes from 1964, once forgotten in storage, were restored and became the heart of the case that followed.

Two trials, in 2001 and 2002, finally brought verdicts for the remaining men the FBI had named. This film follows Addie Mae, her sister Sarah Collins Rudolph, and the long road from silence to justice.

In late February 1957, a four-year-old boy was found in the brush off Susquehanna Road in Fox Chase, Philadelphia, inside a cardboard bassinet box. His hair was freshly cut and his nails were trimmed, yet no one ever reported him missing. For sixty-five years he was known only as the Boy in the Box and America's Unknown Child.

Police recruits searched the area, and the Philadelphia Inquirer printed four hundred thousand flyers that went out with the city's gas bills. Hospital records were checked, leads were followed for decades, and not one led to a name. He was buried in a potter's field and later reburied at Ivy Hill Cemetery.

In 1990 the Vidocq Society took up the case. A forensic reconstruction, DNA from a tooth in 1998, and a new facial reconstruction in 2016 still did not produce a name. In 2019, a second exhumation gave genetic genealogists enough DNA to work with, and a cousin's upload to a public database set off a trail that led to his parents.

A court order for his birth certificate and DNA from living relatives confirmed it. On December 8, 2022, Philadelphia police announced his name, Joseph Augustus Zarelli, and on what would have been his 70th birthday, a new memorial carried his name and image. Around 5:30 p.m., in broad daylight, someone saw her pedaling up the hill on Penny Creek Road. A little later, two people found her in the woods nearby. She did not survive. Her horse's bridle was gone, and it has never been found.

For decades there was no suspect, no witness and no answers. Only the clothes she had been wearing that day, and on one of those borrowed boots, a trace too small for anyone in 1972 to read.
In 2008 a Snohomish County detective sent the boots to the crime lab. Then, on the morning the jury was deciding his fate, he never came back to court.

The next day would have been the day before her 72nd birthday. That morning, the chapel organist found her in the sacristy.

Within ten days detectives had narrowed dozens of names to one: the hospital's own chaplain, Father Gerald Robinson. They took a letter opener shaped like a small silver sword from his quarters. Then, in the middle of his police interview, two powerful men walked into the room and the priest walked out of the station. The reports disappeared. For 24 years, no one was charged.

In 2003 a letter about an entirely different matter brought his name to the Lucas County cold case team. Investigators reopened the evidence, studied the altar cloth, and found a mark that appeared to match the letter opener. In 2006, a Toledo jury reached its verdict.

Three days later she was found in a ditch beside a country road twenty miles away, and one of her shoes was missing.
Then the person responsible did something almost no one in his position ever does. In 1990 a message appeared on the doors of a barn outside the city, asking police a question only he could have known to ask. In 2004, notes sealed in plastic bags were left on the bicycles of little girls, each claiming to come from the same man. His DNA matched across sixteen years, but for three decades no one could put a name to it.
Hundreds of tips. A list of nearly seven hundred names. America's Most Wanted, an FBI command center, and a face predicted from DNA. Nothing worked, until May 2018, when a Fort Wayne detective moved within two weeks of a genetic-genealogy breakthrough in California and a genealogist began building one family tree branch by branch.

Closing arguments began Tuesday in Andrew Griffin’s double-murder trial, where he is accused of killing Thomas Strussion, his former business partner and Strussion’s wife, Angela. Prosecutors argued that money and revenge were at the heart of the killings, pointing to Griffin’s roughly $100K investment in the restaurant business, which he had not recouped. The state emphasized that Griffin entered the victims’ home, demanded money then shot the couple in the head multiple times and staged the scene to look like a robbery gone wrong.

videos.title: Naresh Bhatt GRILLED Over Wife’s Injury Videos
videos.description:
Prosecutors challenged Naresh Bhatt's account of Mamta's alleged fall down the stairs, highlighting the multiple photos and videos she sent him documenting her injuries. During cross-examination, the prosecutor questioned why Mamta went to such lengths to preserve evidence of the incident, asking whether she was trying to make sure it was documented. Bhatt testified that the fall happened sometime between 8 and 9 p.m., but maintained he was not present when she was injured. Prosecutors also replayed a video from inside the couple's home, pointing out the master bathroom and bathtub visible in the footage.

videos.title: You Will Hate The Justice System After Watching This. The Shocking Story of Katie Sepich

On September 1, 2003, 22-year-old graduate student Katie Sepich left a house party in Las Cruces, New Mexico, to walk five blocks home. She never arrived. Her body was found hours later in the desert, and she had fought back so hard that her attacker’s DNA was left beneath her fingernails.

This documentary tells Katie’s story, the 86 days that changed everything, and how her mother Jayann Sepich’s refusal to give up led to Katie’s Law, the DNA-at-arrest laws now used across America.

The man who killed her lived in the basement of the house Milgaard visited that morning, two blocks from the lane. Police interviewed him once in February 1969, as a witness at a bus stop. In 1980 his ex-wife walked into the Saskatoon police station and told officers her paring knife had gone missing the day of the murder. Nothing was done with her statement.

Joyce Milgaard spent a decade fighting for her son. The Supreme Court of Canada freed him in 1992 without clearing him. In 1997, a British laboratory found semen staining on the victim's dress that two earlier analysts had missed, and the profile excluded David Milgaard entirely. videos.title: CALGARY 1976 Cold Case Solved After 48 Years — Four Young Women, Nine Aliases, One Man

#ColdCase #Calgary #DNA

For 48 years, his name was never in the file.

Eva, Patsy, Melissa and Barbara.

🔔 Subscribe to Cold Case Reckoning for Canadian cold cases, forensic breakthroughs and investigations that refused to be forgotten.

On the morning of February 15th, 1976, a man driving toward Cochrane found two fourteen-year-old girls lying side by side on the road beneath the Happy Valley underpass west of Calgary. Eva Dvorak and Patsy McQueen had last been seen walking toward downtown around midnight on Valentine's Day. Both had died of asphyxia. A medical examiner leaned toward a drug-related accident, a coroner's jury could not decide how they died, and a judge at the inquest said the real problem was that girls so young were allowed to run so free.

Seven months later, twenty-year-old Melissa Rehorek was found in a ditch 22 kilometres west of the city, holding a clutch of long black hairs that were not hers. Five months after that, nineteen-year-old Barbara MacLean was found near the Calgary airport with her jacket inside out and the fingers of her left hand bloodied.

More than 800 tips. 500 statements. 853 suspects and persons of interest. More than 600 black-haired men gave hair samples for comparison under a microscope. None of them matched.

In 2003, DNA confirmed that one unknown man had killed both Melissa and Barbara. He became Profile A, and the profile sat in the national DNA data bank without a hit for more than twenty years.

videos.title: TORONTO 1936 Cold Case Solved After 90 Years — DNA Named the Husband Who Buried Her
videos.description:
#ColdCase #Toronto #DNA

For 90 years, nobody knew she was missing.

Mary McLeod Davidson.

🔔 Subscribe to Cold Case Reckoning for Canadian cold cases, forensic breakthroughs and investigations that refused to be forgotten.

On May 18th, 1995, a demolition crew breaking up the concrete floor of a car dealership at 1515 Danforth Avenue found the skeleton of a woman. She had been deliberately buried and struck at least six times in the head. Police could not identify her. For the next 31 years, she was known only as the Danforth Lady.

Tips poured in about women who vanished in the 1940s. None of them matched. She had been in the ground since 1936.

In 2022, her case was selected for the Toronto Police Service's Project 31. Extraction after extraction failed, until a single segment of bone produced a usable DNA profile in November 2024. Genetic genealogy traced her ancestry to the Aberdeen area of Scotland.

In July 2026, police gave her back her name: Mary McLeod Moffat, née Davidson, born in Aberdeenshire in 1905. They also named her husband, Andrew Lloyd Moffat, as the primary suspect in her death. He had abandoned her, secretly married again in Toronto, and ran a tire business on the property next to her grave.

But he had died in 1985 under another name, ten years before she was found.

One woman. Ninety years. One name returned.

In 2025, a family tree built from distant DNA relatives led investigators to Kenneth Smith. Forensic testing subsequently identified Smith as the offender in all three homicides.

Three women. Three decades. One man.

videos.title: OTTAWA 1996 Cold Case Solved After 28 Years — The First Time Ottawa Police Ever Used a Family Tree
videos.description:
#ColdCase #Ottawa #DNA

In the early hours of April 12th, 1996, 22-year-old Christopher Smith was walking home across Ottawa’s Portage Bridge with his cousin after a night out.

He never made it home.

The two men were approached by a stranger and an altercation followed. Christopher was stabbed multiple times. His cousin desperately tried to flag down passing cars while the attacker disappeared from the bridge and into downtown Ottawa.

But the attacker had been injured too.

Roughly a kilometre away, someone stopped at a pay phone on Elgin Street and anonymously called for an ambulance to be sent to the Portage Bridge. When Detective Randy Wisker reached the phone minutes later, the receiver was still swinging.

And there was blood on it.

Police believed the caller was Christopher Smith’s attacker.

They now had something extraordinary: the suspected killer’s voice recorded on an emergency call — and his DNA left on the telephone.

But in 1996, Canada’s National DNA Data Bank did not yet exist. Investigators could compare DNA against someone they already suspected, but they couldn't use that blood to produce the name of a complete stranger.

So the evidence sat preserved.

For 28 years.

The breakthrough came through investigative genetic genealogy — technology capable of turning a DNA profile into something entirely different: a network of distant relatives and, eventually, a family tree.

videos.title: ONTARIO 1975 Cold Case — They Named Her Before They Named Her Killer, 48 Years Later
videos.description:
#ColdCase #Ontario #DNA

For nearly fifty years, Ontario police had a woman’s body, a reconstructed face, and no name.

On May 3rd, 1975, a farmer discovered the body of an unidentified woman in the Nation River near Casselman, Ontario. Investigators found evidence suggesting she had been dropped from the Highway 417 bridge above. But there was nothing at the scene that told them who she was.

She became known simply as the **Nation River Lady**.

Hundreds of kilometres away, a family in Tennessee was desperately searching for 48-year-old businesswoman **Jewell Parchman Langford**, who had travelled to Montreal in April 1975 to live with a younger man named Rodney Nichols. Within days, communication with her family stopped.

Her mother spent years hiring private investigators and contacting authorities. Her brother travelled to Montreal looking for her. But nobody connected the missing woman in Quebec with the unidentified woman recovered from an Ontario river.

For more than four decades, the two investigations existed separately. 

Ontario Provincial Police reconstructed the unidentified woman’s face, established a dedicated tip line and repeatedly appealed to the public. Nothing gave her back her identity.

Then forensic science changed.

In 2019, investigators exhumed the Nation River Lady’s remains and turned to investigative genetic genealogy. Working through distant DNA matches and family trees, investigators eventually reached relatives of a missing Tennessee woman.

videos.title: VANCOUVER 1947 Cold Case — 75 Years Later, DNA Finally Gave Two Little Boys Their Names Back
videos.description:
#ColdCase #Vancouver #DNA

In January 1953, a Vancouver Parks Board worker clearing brush near Beaver Lake in Stanley Park stepped on something beneath the leaves. It was a human skull.

Investigators uncovered the remains of two young children beneath a woman’s fur coat. Beside them were a lunchbox, a single woman’s shoe, a hatchet — and two child-sized leather flying helmets. Police believed the children had died years earlier, around 1947. A doctor identified them as a young boy and girl.

He was wrong.

Both children were boys. That single mistake shaped the investigation for the next forty-five years. Police searched school records, social-service files and missing-person reports for a brother and sister who had never existed, while the real boys remained unidentified.

Their names were Derek D’Alton and David D’Alton.

Derek was seven. David was six. They had lived in Kitsilano, attended Henry Hudson Elementary School, and disappeared from the records decades before anyone connected them to the children found in Stanley Park. Their own family believed they had been taken away by social services.

The breakthrough began when DNA testing finally established that both children were male biological brothers with the same mother but different fathers. Decades later, investigative genetic genealogy allowed detectives to trace their DNA back through a family tree.

At the same time, their great-niece Ally Brady had discovered photographs of two unfamiliar little boys in an old

videos.title: MONTREAL 1975 Cold Case Solved After 48 Years — They Opened a Grave to Prove It
videos.description:
#ColdCaseSolved #ColdCase #DNA

On the Saturday of Easter weekend, 1975, 16-year-old Sharron Prior left her house in Pointe-Saint-Charles, Montreal, to walk five blocks to a pizzeria where her friends were waiting. She had spent the afternoon painting eggs at the kitchen table. She never arrived.

Three days later a beekeeper found her body fifteen miles away, across the river in Longueuil. Beside her in the snow was a man's shirt. Size 17 collar, thirty-four inch sleeves. It was not hers. Detectives concluded it had been used to tie her hands, and then it sat in an evidence box for forty-seven years.

The case had a sketch, a shirt size, a shoe size and a tire track. What it did not have was one police force that owned all of it. Thirteen investigators came and went. More than a hundred suspects were cleared. Her mother, Yvonne Prior, spent forty-eight years refusing to let the file close.

The man who left that shirt was an American truck driver named Franklin Maywood Romine, who fled to Canada on bond in 1974 and died in Montreal in 1982. No DNA database could ever have found him. What found him was the Y chromosome, which passes from father to son almost unchanged, and so does the surname. In May 2023, with a court order from a West Virginia judge, Canadian detectives stood in an Appalachian cemetery and opened his grave.

This documentary covers who Sharron was, the attempted abduction on the same street thirty minutes earlier that nobody connected for forty-seven years,

videos.title: ONTARIO 1984 Cold Case Solved After 36 Years — The Killer Was at the Funeral
videos.description:
#ColdCaseSolved #ColdCase #WrongfulConviction

On October 3rd, 1984, nine-year-old Christine Jessop got off her school bus in Queensville, Ontario, carrying a plastic recorder she had been handed in music class that morning. She brought in the mail, took a nickel from the change dish, and walked to the corner store for a piece of gum. Her mother and brother were about ten minutes behind her.

That gap was twenty minutes long. It was enough.

Eighty-nine days later she was found in a wooded lot in Sunderland, fifty-six kilometres east, with the recorder lying in the grass beside her, her name still on it.

Police arrested her next-door neighbour. Guy Paul Morin was 25, kept honeybees, played clarinet, and had not joined the search. A detective wrote five words in his notebook: "Clarinet player. Weird-type guy." Morin was tried twice, acquitted once, convicted once, and sentenced to life. DNA cleared him in January 1995, ten years after his arrest and eighteen months into a prison term. It remains the most examined wrongful conviction in Canadian history, and it produced a public inquiry, 119 recommendations, and an organisation that still frees people today.

The man who actually did it was on a list the Jessop family gave police in the first week of October 1984. He helped search the fields that autumn. He attended the funeral. He was in the family's living room that night for the wake. He was never interviewed once in thirty-one years, and he was not identified until October

videos.title: ONTARIO 1998 Cold Case Solved After 25 Years — They Built His Face From DNA Before They Had His Name
videos.description:
#ColdCaseSolved #ColdCase #DNA

On January 27th, 1998, 23-year-old Renée Sweeney was working an early shift alone at a video store in a strip mall on Paris Street in Sudbury, Ontario. She was a fourth-year Laurentian University student studying history and music, a trombone player with the Sudbury Symphony Orchestra, and roughly four months from graduating. According to her sister, she was not even scheduled to work that day. She had traded the shift so she would be free for a symphony performance that weekend.

Just after 11 a.m., a man walked in. Renée was attacked and killed. She fought him hard enough to take his skin under her fingernails.

What police recovered that afternoon was more than most homicide investigators ever get. A teal windbreaker and white cotton garden gloves, discarded in the snow behind the plaza and found by a police dog. A bloody fingerprint on the cash tray and a second print underneath it. A running shoe impression in the washroom, invisible until chemically developed. And a complete DNA profile of the killer.

They had everything about him except his name.

Two weeks later, police arrested the wrong man. John Fetterly was charged with first-degree murder on the strength of a misidentified fingerprint and released days later with an apology. He had nothing to do with her death, and twenty-five years later the officers involved confirmed the error under oath.

The case then became the largest criminal investigation in Sudbury's history. More than t

videos.title: QUEBEC 2000 Cold Case Solved After 24 Years — A Discarded Straw at a Cinema Convicted Him
videos.description:
#ColdCaseSolved #ColdCase #DNA

On April 28th, 2000, 19-year-old Guylaine Potvin was found murdered in the basement apartment she shared with other students in Jonquière, Quebec. Her roommates were away that night. A friend who had been with Guylaine the evening before became worried when she stopped answering the phone and went to check on her the following morning.

Guylaine had been sexually assaulted and strangled. Investigators recovered male DNA from multiple pieces of evidence at the scene, but there was a problem: it matched nobody in the police database. There were no witnesses, and despite years of investigation, the identity behind the DNA remained unknown.

For more than two decades, the case remained unsolved.

The breakthrough came in 2022 through a Quebec forensic project known as *Projet Patronyme*. Instead of searching for an exact DNA match, scientists examined the Y chromosome, which is passed down through the male line, to identify surnames potentially associated with the unknown killer's DNA.

One name emerged: Grenon.

Investigators eventually focused on Marc-André Grenon, a man who had once lived in a building behind Guylaine's residence. But a surname wasn't enough to make an arrest. Police still needed his DNA.

So investigators followed him to a cinema.

videos.title: TORONTO 1983 Cold Case Solved After 39 Years — Two Women, Two Neighbourhoods, One Man
videos.description:
#ColdCaseSolved #ColdCase #GeneticGenealogy

On August 17th, 1983, Susan Tice was found murdered in her home on Grace Street in Toronto. She was 45, a nurse turned social worker and a mother of four, and she had moved in barely a month earlier. Four months later, on December 20th, 22-year-old Erin Gilmour was found murdered in her Yorkville apartment above the shop where she worked. She was the daughter of Barrick Gold co-founder David Gilmour.

They lived four kilometres apart. They had never met. Neither had ever met the man who killed them.

Detectives interviewed hundreds of people and cleared every one. The problem was not effort. In 1983, murder investigations assumed the killer was someone the victim knew, so police worked outward through husbands, boyfriends, neighbours and tradespeople. A stranger with no criminal record was not in that haystack at all. In 2000, the new National DNA Data Bank proved one man had killed both women, and then produced nothing, because he had never been convicted of anything.

What finally broke it was investigative genetic genealogy. In 2019, Toronto Police sent crime scene evidence to a Texas lab and got back matches so distant they were fifth and sixth cousins. From that, investigators built eight family trees containing more than 3,000 names, and narrowed it to five brothers from a Cree family with roots on James Bay. videos.title: They Had No Idea Police Already Had Their DNA (5 Cold Cases)
videos.description:
Five men. Five interview rooms. In every case, investigators already had DNA before anyone sat down.

These are real recordings from five cold cases, cut from five full episodes of this channel. Each case was reopened by DNA.

CASE 1 · ORANGE COUNTY, FLORIDA · 1996 → 2021
Terry Paquette, 31, managed a Lil' Champ food store in northwest Orange County. In 2021 detectives questioned Kenneth Stough Jr. after DNA from a discarded bag of beer cans matched blood found in the store. On August 25, 2023, a jury found him guilty of first-degree murder and he was sentenced to life.

CASE 2 · DUNN COUNTY, WISCONSIN · 1974 → 2024
Mary Schlais, 25, was killed on a Wisconsin road in February 1974. The killer left a winter stocking cap. In 2023 genetic genealogy led investigators to Jon Keith Miller, 84. On March 27, 2025, he pleaded no contest to first-degree intentional homicide and was sentenced to life.

CASE 3 · PORT HURON, MICHIGAN · 1980 → 2023
Karen Umphrey, 21, was found dead in November 1980. More than four decades later, DNA from her clothing led detectives to Douglas Laming. On October 10, 2024, a jury found him guilty of first-degree murder; he was sentenced to life without parole. He has never admitted guilt.

CASE 4 · ST. LOUIS, MISSOURI · 1990 → 2022
Robyn Mihan, Donna Reitmeyer, Brenda Pruitt and Sandy Little were killed in 1990. In 2022 DNA from Robyn's case matched Gary Muehlberg, who was already serving life in prison. In March 2023 he pleaded guilty to all four murders.

September 2006. Valley City, North Dakota. A 22-year-old college senior, Mindy Morgenstern, is killed in her apartment. Investigators ask her neighbors for DNA to rule them out. One of them, a county jail officer, gives his willingly, and volunteers to take a polygraph first, to set the example.

What he does not know: by the time he sits down with the examiner, the results are already back.

Built from the recorded polygraph and interview from September 20, 2006, with narration based on court records and news reporting. Moe Gibbs denied the killing in this interview. He was convicted of murder in November 2007 after a second trial and sentenced to life without parole. The North Dakota Supreme Court upheld the conviction in 2009.

videos.description:
Jacksonville, Florida, November 2018. An Eaton County detective walks into a jail interview room and tells Dineane Ducharme he finally found Chris. Three years earlier, she was the one who called police and helped them put a name on a body.

In May 2002, a blueberry farmer between Holland and Grand Haven, Michigan, found a burned metal trunk beside a dirt road. Inside were the remains of a man no one could identify. The Ottawa County Sheriff's Office and Hope College professor David Schock made a documentary about the case, known as "Jack in the Box," in 2005. About ten years later, a woman in Texas watched it online and told detectives the man might be her stepfather, Roberto Caraballo. She said her mother, Beverly McCallum, had done something to him, and she named a friend, Chris, who she said could confirm her story. Investigators found traces of Roberto's blood in the basement of the family's former home in Charlotte, Michigan, and dental records and DNA confirmed his identity. In 2018, the detective found Christopher McMillan, who admitted he had been an accomplice. McMillan pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and testified. In December 2021, a jury convicted Dineane Ducharme of first-degree premeditated murder; she was sentenced to life without parole, and the Michigan Court of Appeals upheld the conviction in 2025. Beverly McCallum was arrested in Rome in 2020, returned to Michigan in 2022, convicted of second-degree murder on April 1, 2024, and sentenced to 40 to 6

videos.title: 60-Year-Old Says His DNA Is in a Lot of Places After 32 Years
videos.description:
Minneapolis, 2015. Cold case detectives sit down with a 60-year-old man and show him a map of a north Minneapolis rail yard. His DNA has already been matched to the 1983 murder of 17-year-old Laurie Mesedahl.

On April 2, 1983, a railroad crew found Laurie Mesedahl between two sets of tracks in a rail yard in north Minneapolis. She had gone to a party the night before and was last seen around 3 a.m. on Bryant Avenue. Investigators kept the evidence, and the case went cold. In 1993, DNA from a 1988 attack on another woman matched Darrell Rea, but by then it was too late to charge that case. In 2013, the state crime lab matched DNA from Laurie's case to the same man. In 2015, Sgt. Chris Karakostas of the Minneapolis police cold case unit and an FBI agent interviewed Rea for nearly five hours. He was told he would be charged by Monday at noon; he was released instead. In September 2017, Hennepin County prosecutors charged him with second-degree murder. He waived a jury, and on May 1, 2019, Judge Tamara Garcia found him guilty. Under the 1983 sentencing guidelines, the maximum was 121 months, and the judge gave him the maximum. In April 2024, FOX 9 reported he was set to be released the following month.

On February 7, 1981, Lt. Ray "Joe" Clark of the Washington County Sheriff's Office was shot through his kitchen window on Dodd's Run Road in Marietta, Ohio. About a year earlier, after a report from Lt. Clark, Mitchell Ruble had lost his badge for excessive force. For 33 years the case stayed cold. He was sentenced to life with parole eligibility after 15 years, and died in prison in February 2017. The conviction was upheld on appeal that August.

On October 10, 2024, a St. Clair County jury found Douglas Laming guilty of first-degree murder. He was sentenced to life without parole in November 2024. A second man, Anthony Harris, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and received 10 to 18 years. Laming has never admitted guilt, and in December 2025 a judge denied his request for a new trial.

videos.description:
Dunn County, Wisconsin, February 15, 1974. Mary Kathleen Schlais, 25, a University of Minnesota honors graduate and artist, left Minneapolis hitchhiking to an art show in Chicago. That afternoon a witness saw a man pulling her body from a car into a snowbank on a dead-end road. She had been stabbed more than a dozen times. The killer left one thing behind: a winter stocking cap.

The DNA on that cap matched no one for fifty years. In 2023, the Investigative Genetic Genealogy Center at Ramapo College built a family tree from it, and the tree ended at Jon Keith Miller, 84, in an assisted-living apartment in Owatonna, Minnesota. On November 7, 2024, Dunn County investigator Dan Westlund knocked on his door with a body camera. This is that recording.

On March 27, 2025, Miller pleaded no contest to first-degree intentional homicide in Dunn County Circuit Court and was sentenced to life in prison.

Real recording of Orange County Sheriff's Office detectives questioning Kenneth Stough Jr. on November 2, 2021. He was 54. Twenty-five years earlier, a store manager named Terry Paquette had been killed. The detectives already had a match.

Terry Paquette was 31. He managed the Lil' Champ food store on Clarcona-Ocoee Road in northwest Orange County, Florida. On Saturday morning, February 3, 1996, he was opening the store. People who drove past noticed the door was locked and the lights were off, though his car was in the lot. Deputies found blood on the outside of the front-door lock. Inside, Terry had been stabbed to death. The cash deposit was gone.

There was other blood in the store that was not Terry's. Investigators believed the killer had injured himself. In 2003 that DNA went into the national database. It matched no one.

In 2019 homicide detective Brian Savelli reopened the file. The state crime lab used genetic genealogy on a bloodstain from a freezer handle, which pointed to three brothers. One of them, Kenneth Stough Jr., had once worked at the store. In 2021 he lived in Eustis, in Lake County. Detectives followed him to a gas station, where he threw a bag of beer cans into a public dumpster. One can matched the blood from the store.

videos.title: 64-Year-Old Has No Idea Police Matched His Straw to a 1979 Murder
videos.description:
Real recordings of a Cedar Rapids police investigator questioning Jerry Burns at his business in Manchester, Iowa, on December 19, 2018. Burns was 64. It was thirty-nine years to the day since Michelle Martinko was killed. The investigator already had his DNA.

Michelle Martinko was 18, a senior at Kennedy High School. On the evening of December 19, 1979, after a choir banquet, she drove alone to Westdale Mall to pay for a winter coat on layaway. She was last seen just before 9 p.m. At 4 a.m. police found her in her family's car in the mall parking lot. She had been stabbed to death. Nothing had been taken.

Police looked at more than 80 suspects. In 2006 a cold-case investigator found blood believed to be the killer's on Michelle's clothing. It matched no one on file. In 2017 a lab built a computer-generated face from that DNA, and a public genealogy database led to three brothers from Manchester. On October 29, 2018, an investigator collected a straw one of them had used. It matched Jerry Burns.

Seven weeks later, on December 19, investigators interviewed him and arrested him that afternoon. Both the interview and the recording from the drive to jail were played for the jury. On February 24, 2020, a Scott County jury found him guilty of first-degree murder. He was sentenced to life without parole. The Iowa Supreme Court upheld the conviction in 2023. In May 2026 Burns filed a new challenge arguing his trial lawyers failed him. That challenge is pending.

videos.description:

videos.title: 77-Year-Old Denies It for Hours Until Detectives Check His Alibi
videos.description:
Real recordings of Fort Worth detectives questioning Glen McCurley in 2020. He was 77. For hours he said he had never seen the girl in the photograph. Then the detectives pointed to his work schedule from 1974.

Carla Walker was 17, a junior at Western Hills High School. In the early hours of February 17, 1974, she was in her boyfriend's car in a bowling alley parking lot after a school dance when a man struck the boyfriend with a pistol and took her. Police found her purse and a pistol magazine. On February 20 her body was found in a culvert near Lake Benbrook.

Police questioned McCurley in 1974 because he owned a .22 Ruger that used the same kind of magazine. He said the gun had been stolen. He passed a polygraph and was cleared. For 46 years nothing changed. In 2019 Fort Worth police reopened the case. Othram, a Texas lab, built a DNA profile from Carla's clothing and used genealogy records to match it to the McCurley family. DNA collected from a trash can outside his home matched.

At trial in August 2021 his attorneys argued the confession was forced from a sick, elderly man. On August 24, 2021 he pleaded guilty to capital murder and was sentenced to life without parole. He died in prison on July 15, 2023.

videos.title: 75-Year-Old Has No Idea Cops Know What He Did 40 Years Ago
videos.description:
Real recordings of Sunnyvale, California detectives arresting Gary Ramirez at his home on Maui on August 2, 2022, and questioning him afterward. He was 75. The detective across the table had known for months what the DNA said.

Karen Stitt was 15, a student at Palo Alto High School. On the night of September 2, 1982 she was in Sunnyvale. The next morning a delivery driver found her behind a cinderblock wall about 100 yards from the bus stop at El Camino Real and Wolfe Road. For almost forty years the case had no suspect.

In 2017 Detective Matt Hutchison took the case. In 2019 he began working with a genetic genealogist, and by 2021 the family tree pointed to one of four brothers from Fresno. In April 2022 DNA collected from discarded trash led to Ramirez, and the Santa Clara County DA's laboratory confirmed it just before the arrest. The operation took months of planning between Santa Clara County, Maui and federal law enforcement and was funded largely by a 2021 Justice Department cold case grant.

On August 10, 2022 Ramirez agreed to be sent back to California. On February 24, 2025 he pleaded no contest to first-degree murder. On May 12, 2025, aged 78, he was sentenced to 25 years to life.

Judy Weaver, 42, managed the Bell-Ness Cafe, a bar on Hewitt Avenue in Everett. On June 1, 1984, after celebrating the bar's sale, she walked home. Just after midnight a passerby saw a fire. Firefighters found Judy in the bedroom of her home on Rucker Avenue; she had been tied up and strangled, and the fire was set to destroy evidence. Her fiancé was suspected for years. He died in 1994. He had nothing to do with it.

In 2020 Everett detectives went back to the evidence. In 2023 DNA from the cords used to tie her wrists matched Mitchell Allen Gaff in CODIS: convicted of attacks in 1979 and 1984, found to be a sexually violent predator, released in 2018, living in Olympia under the name Sam Wise Price. On January 17, 2024 the gum matched.

After his arrest, detectives looked again at the 1980 killing of Susan Vesey, 21, in her home on Casino Road. Her two small children were in the home and were not hurt. Her husband was suspected for more than 40 years and died in July 2025, before anyone was charged. A cord from that scene matched Gaff's DNA. videos.title: 52-Year-Old Has No Idea Police Kept His Bloody Footprints for 26 Years
videos.description:
The real police interview of Jerry Westrom, recorded by the Minneapolis Police Department on February 11, 2019, the day of his arrest, and played for the jury at his trial. He was asked whether he had any idea why detectives wanted to talk to him. "I have no idea," he said. Weeks earlier, detectives had followed him to his daughter's hockey game in Mequon, Wisconsin, and taken the napkin he threw in the trash.

On June 13, 1993, water leaking into a neighbor's unit led staff into Jeanie Childs' apartment in the Horn Towers in south Minneapolis. The shower was still running. Jeanie, 35, had been stabbed about 65 times. She was wearing socks, but there were bare footprints in her blood on the bedroom floor. The case went cold for 26 years.

In 2015, Minneapolis Sgt. Chris Karakostas and an FBI partner reopened it. In 2018 the unknown DNA was uploaded to genealogy databases; in January 2019 a genealogist identified two brothers, and investigators focused on one of them, Jerry Westrom, a 52-year-old businessman and hockey dad from Isanti. The napkin matched the DNA from 1993.

In August 2022, a forensic examiner identified Westrom as the source of three bloody footprints. A Hennepin County jury deliberated for about two hours and found him guilty of first-degree premeditated murder. He was sentenced to life in prison, with possible parole after 30 years under the law of 1993.
